**Exceptions/limits:** An admission cannot be wholly withdrawn if that would prejudice a right it conferred on the opponent; it may only be explained or clarified.; Amendment will not be allowed to substitute a distinct cause of action or case, or to introduce new facts that defeat an accrued right.; Alternative pleas must not be mutually destructive or contradictory of the existing defence in a way that causes irremediable injustice.; Where the amendment is sought after trial commenced, the due-diligence proviso to Order VI Rule 17 applies, though it may be relaxed to correct a description of the property.; Delay and limitation are relevant to discretion but do not remove the power to amend; a disputed limitation bar is left to be decided as an issue.; Where prejudice or delay can be compensated, the amendment is typically conditioned on costs or payment of arrears.; Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is a separate inquiry turning on the acceptability of the explanation and the absence of mala fides.

**Split suggestion:** Treat 1240908_1 (condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act) separately from the amendment-of-pleadings members.

## 10.4 (20 issues)

**Question:** Where a land ceiling law makes a statutorily defined family the unit for applying the ceiling, must land held by each family member (including separated minor sons and spouses holding separately) be aggregated into the family's holding, and is that family-unit approach constitutionally valid?

**Rule:** IF `land_ceiling_law_uses_family_unit and family_defined_by_statutory_relationships and family_member_holds_land and not constitutional_protection_defeated_by_challenge` THEN `family_unit_aggregation_applies_and_is_upheld`

**Definition:** Where a land ceiling statute makes a relationship-based family the ceiling unit, all land held by its members, jointly or separately, is aggregated in the family's holding. That holds even where a minor son has separated by partition or a spouse holds land as separate property. Such a family-unit scheme is not invalid under Article 14 and is protected by Articles 31A and 31B when it is agrarian reform legislation.

- `land_ceiling_law_uses_family_unit`: The applicable agricultural or urban land ceiling statute treats a defined family unit, not each individual member, as the unit for applying the ceiling.
- `family_defined_by_statutory_relationships`: The statute defines the family by listed relationships (for example a person, spouse and minor children) and not by joint title, joint holding or a Hindu joint family.
- `family_member_holds_land`: A person who falls within the statutory family holds land, jointly or separately. This includes a minor son holding after partition, a spouse holding separate or stridhan property, and an adult son treated as a separate unit within an aggregate limit.
- `constitutional_protection_defeated_by_challenge`: A constitutional challenge to the family-unit definition or aggregation succeeds, for example because the law is arbitrary under Article 14 or falls outside the protection of Article 31A or 31B.
- `family_unit_aggregation_applies_and_is_upheld`: The land of all family members is pooled into the family's holding for applying the ceiling, and the family-unit definition and aggregation are not invalidated on the constitutional grounds raised.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 14/20 shown · outliers 6

**Typical outcome:** In all 14 covered members the family-unit scheme prevailed. Six applied the statute to aggregate separated minor sons' land or a wife's separate land. Eight rejected constitutional challenges under Article 14 or the second proviso to Article 31A, largely relying on Articles 31A and 31B.

**Recurring facts:** A ceiling statute defines a family unit as a person, spouse and minor children.; Minor sons hold land separately after a partition made before the appointed day.; A wife holds land in her own name as separate or stridhan property.; Landholders challenge the family-unit definition under Article 14 or Article 31A, or on the ground that adult children and joint families are excluded.; The ceiling law is an agrarian reform measure, often placed in the Ninth Schedule.

**Provisions:** Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act 1973, ss 3(f), 3(o), 4, 5; Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act 1961, s 4(1) and Explanation; Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act, s 6(2); Constitution of India, Arts 14, 19, 31, 31A (including its second proviso), 31B, 39(b)-(c), 367; General Clauses Act 1897, s 3(42); Sections 2(10), 4(1)-(4) and 7(1) Explanation IV of a ceiling statute defining the family by relationship

**Exceptions/limits:** The outcome depends on the particular statute's definition of family and its aggregation clause. Where the statute does not bring a member's separate or self-acquired property into the unit, that property may be excluded (75868557_1, under a differently construed Maharashtra Act).; Transfers made before the statutory cutoff are outside the Act, so land transferred before the cutoff is not aggregated merely because of family relationship.; Adult sons are treated as separate units in some statutes, subject to an aggregate limit on the family and those units (171991274_1).; Aggregation does not extinguish separate ownership. It only determines the ceiling.; Constitutional protection under Articles 31A and 31B applies only to qualifying agrarian reform laws. For urban ceiling laws the Article 14 validity rests on the definition not being arbitrary and not inevitably concentrating wealth.

**Split suggestion:** Split into (a) the family-unit aggregation and constitutional validity group (the 14 covered members), possibly subdivided into statutory construction and constitutional challenge; (b) transfers and the cutoff date (1647440_1, 910696_1, 75868557_1, 1293282_4); (c) urban ceiling and incomplete acquisition (1154981_3); and (d) legitimacy of children of void marriages (391843_3), which belongs to family law.

## 6.3 (20 issues)

**Question:** When may an appellate court (including the Supreme Court) set aside an acquittal, or uphold a conviction entered on reversal of an acquittal, because the acquittal rested on wrongly rejected, ignored or unsound assessment of credible prosecution evidence?

**Rule:** IF `appeal_concerns_acquittal_or_its_reversal and prosecution_evidence_is_credible_and_corroborated and acquittal_rested_on_ignored_or_unsound_grounds and evidence_establishes_guilt_beyond_reasonable_doubt and not evidence_reasonably_supports_two_views` THEN `acquittal_is_set_aside_and_conviction_is_restored_or_upheld`

**Definition:** Appellate courts ordinarily do not disturb an acquittal where two reasonable views are possible. They will set it aside, or uphold a conviction entered on reversal, where the acquittal rested on ignored evidence or perverse, peripheral or speculative grounds and the credible, corroborated evidence establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

- `appeal_concerns_acquittal_or_its_reversal`: The appeal is against an acquittal, or challenges a conviction that a higher court entered by reversing an acquittal.
- `prosecution_evidence_is_credible_and_corroborated`: The court finds the main prosecution evidence (typically eyewitness testimony, or demand and acceptance evidence in corruption cases) reliable and supported by surrounding material such as a prompt report, medical or ballistic evidence, recoveries, motive or the accused's failure to rebut a presumption.
- `acquittal_rested_on_ignored_or_unsound_grounds`: The acquitting court ignored material evidence or relied on perverse, speculative, technical or peripheral grounds such as minor discrepancies, investigative lapses or unsupported defence explanations.
- `evidence_establishes_guilt_beyond_reasonable_doubt`: On the record as a whole, the prosecution has proved the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
- `evidence_reasonably_supports_two_views`: The evidence reasonably permits both a view of guilt and a view of innocence, so the acquittal view is plausible.
- `acquittal_is_set_aside_and_conviction_is_restored_or_upheld`: The acquittal is set aside and the trial court's conviction is restored, or the conviction entered on reversal of the acquittal is upheld.

**Coherence:** high · covered 18/20 shown · outliers 2

**Typical outcome:** In about 17 of 20 members the acquittal was set aside, or the conviction entered on reversal was upheld, and the trial court's conviction was restored or maintained. One member (1330888_1) went the other way and set aside a conviction entered on reversal. One member (1634747_3) restored trial convictions after a High Court reversal that was not an acquittal.

**Recurring facts:** Credible eyewitnesses, often injured or independent, identified the accused as assailants.; A prompt first information report named the accused.; Medical, ballistic or recovery evidence corroborated the eyewitness account.; The acquitting court relied on minor discrepancies, investigative defects, delay or speculative inferences, or ignored material evidence.; Motive or hostility evidence was considered alongside other circumstances.; In the corruption cases, demand, acceptance and recovery of marked money were proved and the presumption was not rebutted.

**Provisions:** Indian Penal Code ss. 302, 34, 149, 147, 148, 307, 323, 304 Part I and II, 299, 447; Code of Criminal Procedure s. 379 with the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act s. 2(a); Arms Act s. 27; Evidence Act s. 3; Prevention of Corruption Act presumption (s. 20)

**Exceptions/limits:** Where the evidence reasonably permits two views, or the trial court's view is at least as acceptable as the reversing court's view, the acquittal stands and a conviction entered on reversal is set aside (as in 1330888_1).; Where the cumulative evidence establishes guilt only against some accused, the acquittal is set aside only as to those accused and left undisturbed for the others (as in 41408_6 and 853471_6).; Interested or injured eyewitness testimony needs assurance from surrounding circumstances or other evidence, as a matter of caution.; In corruption cases, guilt rests on proof of demand and acceptance and on an unrebutted statutory presumption.; Discrepancies on collateral events, investigative omissions or delay do not defeat reliable testimony on the core act, but fundamental conflicts with medical evidence or genuine unreliability of the witnesses can.

## 10.5 (19 issues)

**Question:** Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?

**Rule:** IF `constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and challenge_based_on_omitted_compensation_component and law_within_legislative_competence and (law_protected_by_constitutional_shield or distinct_self_contained_scheme_with_rational_basis_or_public_interest or no_constitutional_or_statutory_requirement_for_omitted_component)` THEN `omission_does_not_invalidate_acquisition_law`

**Definition:** A challenge to an acquisition law for omitting compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation fails where the law is within competence and either a constitutional shield protects it, or it is a distinct scheme with a rational or public-interest basis, or no legal requirement mandates the omitted component. The Court does not read compensation or its additions into legislative entries or into a separate statutory scheme.

- `constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law`: The challenge attacks the validity of a compulsory acquisition law, or an acquisition under it, on constitutional grounds.
- `challenge_based_on_omitted_compensation_component`: The challenge rests on the law's omission of compensation, or of an addition such as solatium, interest or rehabilitation, or on an implied compensation duty said to arise from the legislative entries.
- `law_within_legislative_competence`: The enacting legislature had competence over the subject of acquisition, and the challenge does not show the law to be outside that field.
- `law_protected_by_constitutional_shield`: The law is protected from Part III or Article 31(2) challenge by a constitutional provision such as Article 31(4), 31-A, 31-B, the Ninth Schedule, or the evacuee-property exception in Article 31(5)(b)(iii).
- `distinct_self_contained_scheme_with_rational_basis_or_public_interest`: The law is a separate, self-contained acquisition or compensation scheme whose differences from the general acquisition law rest on an intelligible differentia, or on public interest, and the compensation it provides is not illusory.
- `no_constitutional_or_statutory_requirement_for_omitted_component`: Neither the Constitution nor the governing statute makes the omitted component a condition of valid acquisition, and the law otherwise provides reasonable compensation.
- `omission_does_not_invalidate_acquisition_law`: The omission of the compensation component does not make the law or the acquisition unconstitutional or invalid, and the challenge fails.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 15/19 shown · outliers 4

**Typical outcome:** The challenge fails in all 15 covered members; the omission of compensation or an addition does not by itself invalidate the law. About 7 rest on constitutional protections (Article 31-A, the Ninth Schedule, Article 31(4)). About 5 rest on distinct schemes, reasonable classification or public interest. About 3 hold that the legislative entries or Article 300-A impose no compensation or rehabilitation duty.

**Recurring facts:** The challenger relied on the omission of compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation, often by comparison with the general Land Acquisition Act, 1894.; The law was a special or self-contained scheme (slum clearance, town planning, requisition, evacuee property, inam or estate abolition).; The law was protected by Article 31(4), 31-A or 31-B or by the Ninth Schedule, or had received the President's assent.; Legislative entries on acquisition were said to imply a compensation duty.

**Provisions:** Articles 14, 31(2), 31(4), 31(5)(b)(iii), 31-A, 31-B, 294(b) and 300-A of the Constitution; Entry 36 of List II and entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule; Ninth Schedule and the Seventeenth Amendment; Land Acquisition Act, 1894, ss. 23(2) and 28; Defence of India Act, 1971, ss. 30-31; Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1951, ss. 12-13; Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952

**Exceptions/limits:** The rule does not apply if the law lacks legislative competence.; The rule does not apply if the compensation provided is illusory or unreal; the town-planning member left this open by noting it was not shown.; A law that is not protected by a constitutional shield and does not form a distinct scheme with a rational basis is not saved by this rule.; Where a statute incorporates the general Land Acquisition Act compensation scheme, the omission may be treated differently, as the Nagpur Improvement Trust line is distinguished on this ground.; Where no agreement exists under an evacuee-property law, the law's own compensation provision may make compensation unclaimable. That is a statutory consequence and not a constitutional ground of invalidity.

**Split suggestion:** Separate the covered members into (a) challenges barred by constitutional protections (Article 31-A, 31-B, the Ninth Schedule, Article 31(4), the evacuee-property exception) together with the no-implied-compensation-duty competence cases, and (b) Article 14 and reasonableness challenges to special schemes on solatium, interest or rehabilitation. Treat the four outliers as separate issues: statutory meaning of injurious affection, redetermination classification, colorable legislation, and the nationalization label.

## 19.1 (19 issues)

**Question:** What must the statutory objection-and-hearing procedure before a compulsory land acquisition (chiefly Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894) provide, and what follows when the procedure is or is not complied with?

**Rule:** IF `land_acquisition_proceeding and statutory_objection_procedure_applies and not objection_procedure_validly_dispensed_with and affected_person_filed_objections` THEN `authority_must_give_effective_hearing_and_genuinely_consider_objections_and_non_compliance_invalidates_acquisition`

**Definition:** Where a statute gives landowners a right to object before acquisition and the procedure has not been validly dispensed with, the designated authority (usually the Collector) must give a genuine opportunity to be heard and objectively consider the objections. The government must then independently apply its mind to the objections and the report. Denial of the hearing or mechanical or unproven consideration invalidates the acquisition, but an opportunity that was offered and not used, or whose objections were in fact heard and considered, satisfies the requirement.

- `land_acquisition_proceeding`: The case concerns a compulsory acquisition of land under a statute that provides a procedure for objections.
- `statutory_objection_procedure_applies`: The governing statute gives affected persons a right to object and be heard before the acquisition is finalised (for example Section 5A or an analogous provision).
- `objection_procedure_validly_dispensed_with`: The government has validly dispensed with the objection procedure under an urgency provision.
- `affected_person_filed_objections`: An interested or affected person filed objections to the proposed acquisition within the time allowed.
- `authority_must_give_effective_hearing_and_genuinely_consider_objections_and_non_compliance_invalidates_acquisition`: The designated authority must give the objector a real opportunity to be heard, objectively consider the objections and report, and the government must independently apply its mind before the declaration. Substantial failure to do so vitiates the acquisition, while an opportunity that was actually afforded and not availed of does not.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 15/19 shown · outliers 4

**Typical outcome:** Of the 15 covered members, about 6 invalidated or found the acquisition unsupported for denial of hearing, non-consideration or non-production of records, and about 3 required fuller scrutiny or preserved judicial review. About 6 upheld the acquisition because the hearing was offered, taken up or not proved to be denied, or because the defect caused no prejudice.

**Recurring facts:** Landowners filed written objections to a proposed acquisition under Section 5A or an analogous provision.; The Collector or designated officer heard, or failed to hear, the objectors and reported to the government.; The government made a declaration under Section 6 after considering, or without independently considering, the report.; The State's records or affidavits were sometimes missing or deficient.

**Provisions:** Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 4, 5A, 6 and 17; Article 300A and Article 226 of the Constitution; Railways Act, 1989, Section 20D; Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, Section 52(3); City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, Sections 16 and 17; Article 14 (audi alteram partem); Cantonments Act, 1924, Sections 52 and 185; Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 34

**Exceptions/limits:** The objection procedure may be validly dispensed with under urgency provisions, but the court may still examine whether a bona fide opinion on urgency was formed and may require the State to respond and produce its records.; No violation arises where the objector was notified of a hearing and chose not to appear or to press for a hearing, or could not prove attendance.; A hearing by the government cannot substitute for the hearing the Collector must give.; A defect in the notification, or the lack of a fresh inquiry after an erratum, does not invalidate the acquisition where the owners knew the relevant purpose or participated in the inquiry and suffered no prejudice.; The conclusiveness of the declaration as to need and public purpose does not bar judicial review of the decision-making process, jurisdictional defects or colourable exercise of power.; Rules letting the land-requiring department present its views in the objection inquiry are consistent with the statutory procedure.; Where the State is challenged and fails to produce its records or file a proper affidavit, it cannot show that the objections were considered.

**Split suggestion:** Split into (a) a core group on the content and breach of the Section 5A hearing and consideration requirement (hearing denied, mechanical consideration, missing records, versus hearing given or not availed); (b) judicial review notwithstanding conclusive declarations or urgency dispensation; and (c) the non-acquisition natural-justice cases (building control, urban land ceiling) and the procedural-validity cases (erratum, scheme omission, department rule).

## 30.0 (19 issues)

**Question:** Does a land-related law, tax, compensation scheme or State action in acquisition, release or withdrawal violate the equality guarantee of Article 14 when it treats similarly situated persons or properties differently (or dissimilar ones alike) without an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law?

**Rule:** IF `equality_challenge_to_land_related_law_or_state_action and (similarly_situated_persons_or_properties_treated_differently or dissimilar_persons_or_properties_treated_alike) and not (classification_rests_on_intelligible_differentia_with_rational_nexus_to_object) and no_valid_justification_shown_by_state` THEN `measure_violates_article_14_and_is_invalid_to_that_extent`

**Definition:** Under Article 14, a land-related law or State action is invalid if it treats similarly situated owners, parcels, properties or groups differently, or treats materially dissimilar ones alike, without an intelligible differentia that is rationally related to the law's object and without any justification from the State. Where the discrimination is in executive action (selective acquisition, release or withdrawal), the State must treat comparable owners consistently or the action is set aside.

- `equality_challenge_to_land_related_law_or_state_action`: The challenge is under Article 14 to a statute, rule, tax, assessment, compensation provision, or an executive act concerning acquisition, release, withdrawal, ceiling or assessment of land or buildings.
- `similarly_situated_persons_or_properties_treated_differently`: Owners, creditors, factories, parcels or other subjects that are alike in relation to the law's object receive different treatment, such as different compensation, selection for acquisition, exemption, release, or procedure.
- `dissimilar_persons_or_properties_treated_alike`: Materially different properties or persons (for example, buildings or land differing in use, quality, productivity or location) are subjected to the same uniform tax, assessment or standard without rational classification.
- `classification_rests_on_intelligible_differentia_with_rational_nexus_to_object`: The classification is founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded, and that differentia bears a rational relation to the object the law seeks to achieve.
- `no_valid_justification_shown_by_state`: The State has not explained or shown, in the law or surrounding circumstances, a valid basis for the differential or uniform treatment; the presumption of constitutionality does not supply an undisclosed basis.
- `measure_violates_article_14_and_is_invalid_to_that_extent`: The law or action is held to violate Article 14 and is struck down, quashed or declared void, in whole or to the extent of the discriminatory provision (subject to severability), or equal treatment is directed.

**Coherence:** high · covered 19/19 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 19 members the challenged law or State action was held to violate Article 14 and was struck down, quashed or declared void (in whole or as applied to the affected lands), or equal treatment was directed (for example, same withdrawal treatment, statutory solatium).

**Recurring facts:** Landowners or properties alike in relation to the law's object receive different compensation, assessment, selection, exemption or release.; The State offers no explanation, or an explanation unrelated to the law's objective, for the differential treatment.; Special or modified acquisition regimes give lower compensation or fewer rights than the ordinary acquisition law for the same public purpose.; Uniform tax or assessment bases (floor area, flat minimum rates) are applied to materially dissimilar buildings or land.; Artificial family definitions or progressive compensation slabs produce unequal burdens among similarly placed landholders.; Executive release or withdrawal from acquisition is granted to some owners but denied or arbitrarily given to comparable ones.

**Provisions:** Article 14 of the Constitution; Article 19(1)(f) (as it then stood); Articles 13(2), 265 and 31-A; Land Acquisition Act, 1894, sections 23(2) and 48; U.P. Nagar Mahapalika Adhiniyam, 1959

**Exceptions/limits:** Valid classification: differential treatment is upheld where it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object; fiscal laws allow the legislature wider latitude in classification.; The presumption of constitutionality cannot supply a basis that does not appear in the law or surrounding circumstances.; Where the discriminatory provisions are integral to the scheme and cannot be severed, the wider law or chapter falls (at least as applied to the affected lands); otherwise invalidity may be confined to the offending provision.; Negative equality: a person cannot claim repetition of an unlawful benefit given to others; the equality claim in withdrawal or release cases succeeds only where the comparators were lawfully treated and the State alleges no illegality.; No equality claim arises where the acquisition and vesting predated the Constitution.; Separate opinion in one member (progressive compensation) treated ability to bear loss as a relevant basis and would have upheld the rates.; Some members also rest on additional grounds (the former Article 19(1)(f), absence of hearing); these are not necessary for the core Article 14 rule.

## 5.6 (19 issues)

**Question:** When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?

**Rule:** IF `eviction_proceeding_under_statutory_scheme and invoked_ground_conditions_established and additional_requirement_invoked_by_opponent and (requirement_not_part_of_invoked_ground or invoked_scheme_overrides_requirement)` THEN `additional_requirement_need_not_be_satisfied`

**Definition:** Where eviction is sought on a statutory ground or special procedure whose own conditions are met, a further requirement or protection drawn from another provision or statute need not be satisfied if it is not part of that ground, is expressly excepted, or is displaced by the invoked scheme's overriding or later special character.

- `eviction_proceeding_under_statutory_scheme`: The case is an eviction or recovery-of-possession proceeding (or its execution) under a rent-control, accommodation-control or public-premises statute.
- `invoked_ground_conditions_established`: The conditions the statute itself prescribes for the ground or special procedure actually invoked (for example bona fide need, a listed ground, the prescribed certificate, or public premises with an unauthorised occupant) have been pleaded and proved, or are otherwise satisfied.
- `additional_requirement_invoked_by_opponent`: The tenant or occupant relies on a further requirement or protection, such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of ownership, a pleading requirement, residential-only letting, a rehousing duty, or protection under another tenancy law.
- `requirement_not_part_of_invoked_ground`: On the statutory text and structure, the further requirement does not form part of the invoked ground. It may be expressly excepted for that ground, apply only to a different ground, arise only at a later stage, or be answered by estoppel or by a finding that the ground rests in substance on another basis.
- `invoked_scheme_overrides_requirement`: The invoked special or later statutory scheme, by a non obstante clause, its purpose and policy, or its later and more specific character, prevails over the inconsistent requirement or protection in the other law.
- `additional_requirement_need_not_be_satisfied`: The landlord or authority may obtain or execute eviction without complying with the further requirement, and the opponent's objection based on it fails.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 18/19 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In all 18 covered members the landlord or authority prevails because the extra requirement is held inapplicable or displaced. About 6 members resolve a conflict with slum-area permission, 2 resolve a conflict with rent-control protection in favour of public premises, 2 or 3 address the District Magistrate's permission, 3 address comparative hardship, 2 address title and estoppel, and 2 address reconstruction.

**Recurring facts:** A landlord or public authority seeks eviction on a specific statutory ground such as bona fide need, wilful non-payment, unlawful subletting, material alteration, or unauthorised occupation of public premises.; The tenant or occupant invokes an extra hurdle: prior slum-area or District Magistrate permission, comparative hardship, proof of title, a rehousing duty, or rent-control protection.; The invoked scheme has a non obstante clause, is later or more specific in time, or is expressly excepted from the hurdle.

**Provisions:** Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, ss. 14(1)(e), 14A, 25A-25C, 14(7), 14, 3(a), 50, 54; Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act 1956, ss. 19 and 39; Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act 1971, including s. 15; U.P. Cantonments (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1952, s. 14(1); U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act 1947, s. 3(1); Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947, ss. 13(1)(g), 13(2), 13A-1; Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, ss. 12(1)(f), 12(1)(h), 18; Karnataka Rent Control Act 1961, s. 21(4); East Punjab Urban Land Restriction Act 1949, s. 13-B; Evidence Act 1872, s. 116

**Exceptions/limits:** The invoked ground's own conditions must still be proved, for example bona fide need (a service certificate does not itself prove it), a listed ground, or the statutory ownership period.; Estoppel against denying title does not apply where the tenant shows attornment to a paramount title holder or the landlord's subsequent loss of title.; Overriding effect applies only to the extent of actual inconsistency, and conflicts between non obstante clauses are resolved by language, purpose and policy.; Statutory restrictions that are part of the invoked ground itself still apply. An example is the statutory postponement of executing a residential-need eviction order, which operates automatically by law, even if the order does not recite it.; Where the order is truly based on the ground that carries the extra duty (for example solely on reconstruction), that duty is not displaced.

**Split suggestion:** If a tighter rule is needed, split into: (1) overriding special or later law over slum-area permission or tenant-protection law (1220782_2, 1575265_1, 768853_1, 823591_1, 6571_2, 6571_3, 453977_4); (2) permission exempted for listed or independent grounds (1664566_2, 1821913_2, 1073776_1); (3) comparative hardship not required (1053321_4, 1094547_4, 829250_2); (4) title, ownership and estoppel (109405390_1, 1254746_1); (5) the ground's own scope, covering reconstruction versus personal need and mixed use (1002519_1, 152387_2, 1187427_2). Place 1319723_2 separately.

## 1.8 (19 issues)

**Question:** When can an accused who pleads private defence (of person or property) establish that right, given who was the aggressor, whether there was a reasonable apprehension of danger, the weapons carried, the injuries on each side, and the credibility of the defence account?

**Rule:** IF `criminal_case_with_private_defence_plea and not accused_proved_or_made_probable_reasonable_apprehension_of_danger_justifying_force_used and (accused_found_to_be_aggressors_or_initiated_attack or defence_account_improbable_or_unsupported_by_evidence or injuries_on_accused_alone_without_corroborating_circumstances or force_used_deadly_and_disproportionate_to_threat_posed_by_unarmed_opponents)` THEN `private_defence_not_established_and_plea_rejected`

**Definition:** A plea of private defence fails where the accused do not show, on the evidence and circumstances, a reasonable apprehension of danger justifying the force used. This typically happens where the accused were the aggressors, their account is improbable or unsupported, injuries alone are relied on, or deadly force was used against unarmed opponents posing no serious threat.

- `criminal_case_with_private_defence_plea`: The accused in a criminal trial or appeal claims that their violent act was justified by the right of private defence of person or property.
- `accused_proved_or_made_probable_reasonable_apprehension_of_danger_justifying_force_used`: On the evidence and surrounding circumstances (including by relying on prosecution evidence), the accused has shown it probable that they faced a reasonable apprehension of danger, such as death or grievous hurt where death was caused, that justified the force used.
- `accused_found_to_be_aggressors_or_initiated_attack`: The courts found on the evidence that the accused, often armed and prepared, started the confrontation or attack rather than responding to an attack by the other side.
- `defence_account_improbable_or_unsupported_by_evidence`: The accused's version of the incident (for example that the other side attacked first or was armed) is implausible, speculative, contradicted by eyewitness or physical evidence, or lacks any supporting material, including about how the accused were injured.
- `injuries_on_accused_alone_without_corroborating_circumstances`: The only basis for the plea is injuries on the accused or their associates, and these were simple, unexplained as to cause or timing, or not linked to an attack by the victim, so the circumstances do not make the defence probable.
- `force_used_deadly_and_disproportionate_to_threat_posed_by_unarmed_opponents`: The accused used lethal or grievous force, such as firearms or edged weapons, against opponents who were unarmed, fleeing, trespassing without a threat to life, or otherwise posed no threat of death or grievous hurt.
- `private_defence_not_established_and_plea_rejected`: The right of private defence is held not established, or exceeded, and the plea is rejected, so the conviction is upheld or sustained to that extent.

**Coherence:** high · covered 19/19 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 19 members the private-defence plea (or the related claim that the complainant side was the aggressor) was rejected or held exceeded, and convictions were upheld or maintained. One member (1736620_1) found a right to remove a trespasser but held it exceeded, and one (1355674_2) found the accused were aggressors, so the opponents' counter-force was justified.

**Recurring facts:** Accused arrived armed (firearms, lathis, spears, knives) against unarmed or less-armed opponents, often in land or property disputes.; Accused relied on injuries to themselves or associates, which were simple, superficial, unexplained or not linked to the victim's attack.; Eyewitness, medical or physical evidence (blood, absence of weapons at the scene, injury patterns) contradicted the defence version.; Concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court rejecting the plea.; Deadly force used where no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt existed.

**Provisions:** Indian Penal Code Sections 96-106, especially 96, 97, 99, 100, 102, 103, 104, 105; IPC Section 441 (criminal trespass); IPC Sections 302 and 304(1); CrPC Section 313; Section 117 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1939 (revenue entry presumption)

**Exceptions/limits:** The accused need only make the plea probable on a balance of probabilities and may rely on prosecution evidence or circumstances without examining defence witnesses; if that standard is met, the plea can succeed.; Injuries on the accused do not by themselves establish private defence, but they can matter when the surrounding circumstances (nature, timing, cause, who was the aggressor) corroborate the defence account.; Where an accused in possession of property faces a trespasser, force to remove the trespasser is allowed, but causing death is not justified against ordinary criminal trespass without apprehension of death or grievous hurt; the right is then exceeded rather than wholly absent.; Where there is a concurrent factual finding by the courts below that the claimants were the aggressors, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily disturb it.; Failure to raise the plea expressly in a Section 313 CrPC statement does not bar the court from considering it on the surrounding circumstances.

## 7.5 (19 issues)

**Question:** Does a person who qualifies as a tenant under a protective tenancy or rent-control statute keep tenant status and protection against eviction after a general-law event (expiry of a fixed term, termination, an eviction decree, absence of an allotment order, or the lessor's death), so that eviction is possible only on a statutory ground and through the prescribed process?

**Rule:** IF `statutory_tenancy_regime_applies and occupant_within_statutory_tenant_definition and general_law_event_would_otherwise_end_tenancy and not (statutory_eviction_ground_established or tenancy_ended_by_prescribed_statutory_process) and not statute_expressly_excludes_occupant` THEN `tenant_status_and_statutory_protection_continue_and_eviction_only_by_statutory_process`

**Definition:** Where a protective tenancy statute defines tenant to cover a person who continues in possession, or otherwise covers the occupant, the end of the contractual or general-law tenancy does not remove tenant status. The tenant stays protected and can be evicted only on the statute's grounds and by its procedure, and a civil claim or decree resting only on expiry, termination or a similar event fails.

- `statutory_tenancy_regime_applies`: A protective land-tenancy or rent-control statute governs the premises or land and restricts eviction of tenants.
- `occupant_within_statutory_tenant_definition`: The occupant falls within the statute's definition of tenant, for example because the definition includes a person continuing in possession after termination, a person from whom rent is payable, or a cultivating tenant.
- `general_law_event_would_otherwise_end_tenancy`: A general-law event has occurred that would end or defeat the tenancy outside the statute, such as expiry of a fixed term, notice of termination, an eviction decree, a lease made without an allotment order, a lessor's death, or letting out of structures on the land.
- `statutory_eviction_ground_established`: The landlord has proved one of the grounds on which the statute permits eviction.
- `tenancy_ended_by_prescribed_statutory_process`: The tenancy has been ended by a lawful eviction, relinquishment, or termination carried out in the manner the statute prescribes (for example the designated revenue authority or required permission or notice).
- `statute_expressly_excludes_occupant`: The statutory definition or a provision expressly excludes the occupant, for example a person against whom an eviction decree has already been made.
- `tenant_status_and_statutory_protection_continue_and_eviction_only_by_statutory_process`: The occupant remains a tenant with the statute's protection, and the landlord can recover possession only on a statutory ground through the prescribed procedure.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 14/19 shown · outliers 5

**Typical outcome:** In about 13 of the 14 covered members, the tenant or heirs were held to retain tenant status and protection, and eviction, execution or the civil suit failed or was barred. The exception is the Karnataka company, where continued tenancy led to a statutory vesting in the State. The outliers mostly concern heritability or timing and also favour the tenant or heirs.

**Recurring facts:** A tenant stayed in possession after a lease expired, a tenancy was terminated, or an eviction decree was passed.; The landlord sought possession by a civil suit, execution, or ejectment without a statutory ground or the prescribed procedure.; The statutory definition of tenant included a person continuing in possession or a person paying rent.; Some tenants died and their heirs claimed continued protection.; The lease was made without an allotment order, or the lessor was a life-estate holder who died.

**Provisions:** Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act 1953, ss 2(6), 9, 14-A, with Punjab Tenancy Act 1887, ss 4(5), 40; East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, ss 2(i), 13(1); Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, ss 2(1)(ii), 14; Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1950, ss 3(vii), 13(1); Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, ss 2(i), 14; U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act 1947, ss 2(g), 3(1); Karnataka Land Reforms Act, ss 5, 6, 79-B; Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, s 11(1); Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act 1955, ss 2(aa), 3; Non-agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act 1955, s 5(1)(a); Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss 106, 116; Rent Act s 21(1) and s 3(r) (statute not named in the member)

**Exceptions/limits:** The rule yields where the statute expressly excludes the occupant, for example a person already subject to an eviction decree under that Act's own definition.; It does not apply once a statutory eviction ground is proved or the tenancy is ended by the prescribed process, such as court eviction or relinquishment.; Protection depends on the particular statute's wording, so the same facts can give different results under different statutes. The Karnataka land-reform member shows that continued tenancy can also trigger statutory consequences adverse to the tenant, here a company's prohibition on holding agricultural land.; A statute that expressly restricts succession or imposes qualifications can limit the protection passing to heirs. Prospective amendments do not divest rights vested before they took effect.; One member (107607168_1) expressed its view in conflict with an earlier decision and referred the point to a larger Bench, so the point is not settled.

**Split suggestion:** Split into (a) survival of tenant status and protection after expiry, termination, decree or lack of allotment, which is the core group; (b) heritability and succession to tenancy (1327310_1, 1887042_1, 1584099_1, 1327310_2, 158115_1, 1464257_3, 390420_3); and (c) statutory rights and conditions of tenants such as purchase of proprietary rights, notice at the agricultural year end, and non-forfeiture on letting out (165933_2, 1323567_1, 1385220_2, 1879186_2).

## 5.7 (19 issues)

**Question:** In a summary eviction proceeding where the tenant must obtain leave to contest or defend, when must the Controller or court grant leave, and when may it refuse leave?

**Rule:** IF `summary_eviction_leave_stage and tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_that_if_established_could_disentitle_landlord and not defence_is_bare_vague_sham_or_outside_statutory_grounds` THEN `leave_to_contest_must_be_granted`

**Definition:** In summary eviction proceedings, leave to contest must be granted where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts which, if proved, could disentitle the landlord from possession and which raise a genuine triable issue. The leave stage concerns disclosure, not proof, so the Controller must not decide disputed facts on affidavits. Leave may be refused where the defence is bare, vague, sham, estopped or irrelevant to the statutory grounds.

- `summary_eviction_leave_stage`: The landlord seeks possession through a special or summary rent-control procedure in which the tenant must apply, usually by affidavit, for leave to contest or defend.
- `tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_that_if_established_could_disentitle_landlord`: The tenant's application or affidavit states facts, as opposed to proof, which if accepted at trial could defeat a ground the landlord must establish, such as bona fide need, absence of alternative accommodation, ownership or landlord status, the existence of a tenancy, or the purpose of letting. These facts raise a genuine triable issue.
- `defence_is_bare_vague_sham_or_outside_statutory_grounds`: The tenant's defence consists of bare or unsupported assertions, is illusory, frivolous or contradicted by the tenant's own sworn position, or rests on matters that cannot defeat the statutory ground for recovery.
- `leave_to_contest_must_be_granted`: The Controller or court must give the tenant leave to contest or defend, and the dispute is then decided after the tenant is allowed to contest and prove the defence. Leave may be conditional, for example on depositing arrears of rent.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 13/19 shown · outliers 6

**Typical outcome:** In 13 covered members, leave was granted or held required in about 9 (1025530_1, 1187427_4 as the test, 1323229_1, 1331869_1, 1331869_5, 158079666_1, 1594520_1, 370236_1, 378172_1; 1977447_2 states the same test). Leave was refused or the refusal upheld in 3 where the defence was vague, sham or irrelevant (1020200_2, 141468481_2, 171435_2). The remaining member (1977447_2) states the test and confines it to the statutory grounds.

**Recurring facts:** The landlord seeks summary eviction, most often for bona fide personal or residential need.; The tenant files an affidavit seeking leave to contest or defend.; The tenant disputes need, alternative accommodation, ownership or landlord status, the existence of a tenancy, or the purpose of letting.; The Controller refused leave after deciding disputed facts on affidavits, or on vague or unsupported assertions.

**Provisions:** Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, sections 14(1)(e), 14A, 25B(4), 25B(5) and related sub-sections; East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, sections 13-B, 18-A(4) and 18-A(5); Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1982, section 14(4) and (5); Order XXXVII CPC, rejected as an analogue; Order XII Rule 6 CPC (outlier members)

**Exceptions/limits:** Leave is not granted on mere assertion. Unsupported allegations about alternative accommodation, or grounds outside the matters the landlord must establish, do not suffice.; A defence contradicted by the tenant's own sworn acknowledgment, or found sham, illusory or moonshine, does not raise a triable issue.; Where the special provision confines the inquiry to specific statutory grounds (for example section 14A or section 13-B), only facts negating those grounds count.; The test is not the Order XXXVII CPC 'substantial defence' test. It is narrower and focused on disclosure of facts that could disentitle the landlord.; Leave may be made conditional on depositing arrears and continuing to pay rent.

**Split suggestion:** Keep the 13 leave-to-contest members as the core cluster. Move the three Order XII Rule 6 judgment-on-admission members (109034285_1, 94788381_1, 62368827_2) into a separate cluster on summary decrees on admissions where a material defence is disputed. Treat 1178802_3 and 562631_3 (burden of proof on discretion or hardship) and 1872012_2 (revision procedure) as separate singletons.

## 29.1 (19 issues)

**Question:** When may a court permit amendment of a pleading in a pending civil proceeding under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, in particular where the amendment supplies particulars, adds or alters relief, or is sought after limitation has expired, without changing the nature of the suit or causing irremediable prejudice?

**Rule:** IF `pleading_amendment_application_in_pending_civil_proceeding and amendment_necessary_to_determine_real_controversy and not amendment_changes_nature_of_suit_or_substitutes_new_cause_of_action and not opposing_party_suffers_irremediable_prejudice_beyond_costs and (amendment_stage_is_pretrial or due_diligence_shown_or_amendment_is_formal_on_pleaded_facts)` THEN `amendment_should_be_allowed_on_terms`

**Definition:** Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, courts take a liberal approach and allow amendments that are needed to decide the real controversy, provided they do not change the nature of the suit or introduce a new cause of action and do not cause prejudice that costs cannot cure. Expiry of limitation, delay, or a resulting change in forum or valuation does not by itself bar the amendment; these are factors in the court's discretion, and a disputed limitation question can be left for trial.

- `pleading_amendment_application_in_pending_civil_proceeding`: A party has applied to amend a plaint or other pleading in a civil suit or proceeding that is still pending.
- `amendment_necessary_to_determine_real_controversy`: The proposed amendment helps decide the real questions in controversy between the parties, for example by supplying particulars, completing or correcting the relief, or covering related events or disputes already in issue.
- `amendment_changes_nature_of_suit_or_substitutes_new_cause_of_action`: The amendment would change the basic nature or subject matter of the suit or replace the existing cause of action with a distinct one.
- `opposing_party_suffers_irremediable_prejudice_beyond_costs`: The amendment would cause the other side injury that cannot be compensated by costs, such as taking away an accrued right or defence, or leaving the other side unable to meet the amended case.
- `amendment_stage_is_pretrial`: The application was made before the trial began.
- `due_diligence_shown_or_amendment_is_formal_on_pleaded_facts`: If the trial has begun, the party shows that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence, or the amendment only formalises relief on facts already pleaded and tried.
- `amendment_should_be_allowed_on_terms`: The court should permit the amendment, usually subject to costs and to giving the opponent an opportunity to respond, for example by an additional written statement.

**Coherence:** high · covered 18/19 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In about 18 of 19 members the amendment is allowed, often subject to costs and a chance for the opponent to respond, and orders refusing it are set aside. The remaining member sets aside an unnecessary remand after a formal amendment.

**Recurring facts:** A plaintiff seeks to add or alter relief, such as declaration, possession, redemption, damages or a formal declaration, in a pending suit.; The facts supporting the amendment are already pleaded, or the amendment only supplies particulars or corrects wording.; Lower courts refused the amendment on grounds of limitation, change in the nature of the suit, or delay, and the Supreme Court reversed them.; The application was often made before trial, and the defendant could file an additional written statement.; Allowing the amendment would avoid a separate suit or multiplicity of proceedings.

**Provisions:** Order VI Rule 17 CPC; Order VI Rule 2 CPC; Order I Rule 1 CPC; Section 16(c) Specific Relief Act, 1963; Order XXI Rules 97, 99 and 103 CPC; Section 39 U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972; Leading cases: Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil; L.J. Leach v. Jardine Skinner; Charan Das v. Amir Khan; A.K. Gupta v. Damodar Valley Corp.; B.K.N. Pillai v. P. Pillai; Pankaja v. Yellappa; Revajeetu Builders

**Exceptions/limits:** Amendment is refused where it introduces a new or different cause of action or changes the basic nature of the suit.; Amendment is refused where it sets up a fresh time-barred claim and deprives the opponent of a defence or accrued right that costs cannot compensate.; Where the application is made after trial has commenced, the proviso requires that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence, unless the amendment is purely formal on facts already pleaded and tried.; Amendment is not a matter of right; the court has discretion and does not decide the merits of the amended claim at the amendment stage.; Amendment should not be allowed where it withdraws an admission that gave the other side a right.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally, treat 1533893_5 (remand after a formal amendment) separately, and treat the limitation-specific members (104860043_2, 1732740_3, 301256_1) as a sub-cluster on limitation and new cause of action.

## 10.6 (19 issues)

**Question:** When is a land-reform or resource-distribution law (or the constitutional amendment protecting it) immune from challenge under the equality, freedom and property provisions of the Constitution, and what connection to agrarian reform or to distribution of material resources for the common good is needed for that immunity?

**Rule:** IF `constitutional_challenge_to_law_or_amendment and law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform_or_gives_effect_to_distribution_of_community_resources_for_common_good and required_nexus_or_dominant_purpose_shown and applicable_protective_provision_conditions_met` THEN `law_is_protected_from_fundamental_rights_and_basic_structure_challenge`

**Definition:** A law that is genuinely part of agrarian reform, or gives effect to the distribution of community material resources for the common good, is shielded from equality, freedom and property challenges (and does not offend the basic structure) once the required nexus and the formal conditions of the protective provision are met. The shield does not extend to acquisitions unconnected with agrarian reform.

- `constitutional_challenge_to_law_or_amendment`: The validity of a land-related statute, rule or constitutional amendment is challenged as violating equality, freedom, property rights or the basic structure.
- `law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform_or_gives_effect_to_distribution_of_community_resources_for_common_good`: The measure, judged by substance and dominant purpose, is agrarian reform (for example land ceilings, surplus-land redistribution, tenancy reform, common-purpose reservation, vesting of estates or grants) or gives effect to distributing the community's material resources for the common good.
- `required_nexus_or_dominant_purpose_shown`: The law has a real, not fanciful, connection to the agrarian-reform or common-good distribution objective, and any ancillary provisions merely support that dominant purpose; a broad view of 'distribution' (allocation, allotment, apportionment) is taken.
- `applicable_protective_provision_conditions_met`: The formal conditions of the relevant protective provision are satisfied (for example presidential assent where required, the subject matter falling within the protected category such as an estate, jagir or inam, or the law being a protected amendment), and no express declaration is needed where the law's contents show the policy.
- `law_is_protected_from_fundamental_rights_and_basic_structure_challenge`: The law cannot be successfully challenged under the covered fundamental rights (equality, freedom, property/compensation), and it does not damage the basic structure.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 17/19 shown · outliers 2

**Typical outcome:** About 15 of 17 covered members uphold the law or amendment as protected agrarian reform or common-good distribution and reject the challenge. 1634289_1 holds that a housing-acquisition law unconnected with agrarian reform is not protected. 1576124_2 is a definitional step holding that a jagir or inam grant is an estate. Two outliers on acquisition safeguards are excluded.

**Recurring facts:** Land ceilings, surplus-land acquisition and redistribution to landless tillers or agriculturists; Vesting of estates, jagirs, inams, janmam rights or forests in the State as part of land reform; Consolidation or village-planning reservation of land for common purposes without compensation; Petitioners invoking Articles 14, 19 and 31 or the basic structure against the reform; Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule or enacted with presidential assent

**Provisions:** Article 31A (including 31A(1)(a) and 31A(2)(a)); Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule; Article 31C; Article 39(b) and 39(c); Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 and 300A; Article 368 and Article 13(2); Entry 18 of List II and Entry 42 of List III; Ranjit Singh, Kochuni, Kesavananda Bharati, Waman Rao, Minerva Mills and Sanjeev Coke

**Exceptions/limits:** Protection for estate-acquisition laws applies only where the measure is connected with agrarian reform; a bare transfer of rights or acquisition for unrelated purposes such as general housing schemes is not protected.; A merely fanciful connection to agrarian-reform or rural-welfare purposes is insufficient; land used for unrelated purposes may be restrained.; Where the protective provision requires presidential assent, it must have been obtained.; Laws outside the protected categories remain subject to ordinary constitutional requirements, for example public purpose and compensation for acquisition of State-owned property, and statutory safeguards in emergency acquisition (on which the judges differed and the matter was referred to a larger Bench).; Challenges to the protective constitutional provision itself are tested only against the basic structure, and the right to property is not a basic feature.

**Split suggestion:** Keep a core group on agrarian-reform and common-good protection under Articles 31A and 31C. Optionally separate the basic-structure amendment cases (799151_1, 1515136_4, 553582_1) and the estate-definition cases (1576124_2, 1576124_3). Move 56073873_7 and 603736_4 to a separate cluster on constitutional safeguards for compulsory acquisition and deprivation of property.

## 54.0 (19 issues)

**Question:** Does an existing tenancy or subordinate interest continue despite an intervening event (partial acquisition of the reversion, merger of interests, statutory abolition or vesting, a termination notice or pending possession proceeding, a third-party title suit, or wrongful dispossession) that does not satisfy the legally prescribed requirements for ending it?

**Rule:** IF `existing_tenancy_or_subordinate_interest and intervening_event_occurred and not event_satisfies_legal_requirements_for_termination and not clear_intention_or_express_statutory_provision_ending_interest` THEN `tenancy_or_subordinate_interest_continues`

**Definition:** An existing tenancy or subordinate interest is not ended by a partial acquisition of the reversion, a unity of holding of non-higher/lower interests, abolition or vesting, a termination notice or pending proceeding, a third-party title suit, or wrongful dispossession, unless the legally prescribed mode of termination is completed or a clear intention or an operative statutory provision ends it. The tenant's statutory rights and obligations therefore continue.

- `existing_tenancy_or_subordinate_interest`: A valid tenancy, lease or subordinate interest (such as a raiyati interest) existed when the intervening event occurred.
- `intervening_event_occurred`: An event occurred that is said to end the tenancy: a partial acquisition of the reversion or a unity of holding, abolition or vesting of the landlord's interest, a termination notice or pending possession or ejectment proceeding, a suit by a superior claimant, a change in the landlord's identity, or wrongful dispossession.
- `event_satisfies_legal_requirements_for_termination`: The event meets the conditions the governing law sets for ending a tenancy, such as vesting of the lessor's and lessee's interests in the whole property in one person at the same time and in the same right, an order or decree of the competent authority, or the commencement of a provision extinguishing the relationship.
- `clear_intention_or_express_statutory_provision_ending_interest`: The parties' clear intention to merge or end the interest is shown, or a statutory provision already in force expressly extinguishes the landlord-tenant relationship.
- `tenancy_or_subordinate_interest_continues`: The tenancy or subordinate interest remains subsisting, with the tenant's rights and obligations (including statutory purchase, pre-emption or rent-control rights and duties) unaffected by the event.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 16/19 shown · outliers 3

**Typical outcome:** In all 16 covered members the tenancy or subordinate interest was held to continue, so the tenant kept eviction protection, purchase or pre-emption rights, or rent-control obligations. About 7 of these turn on the Transfer of Property Act merger doctrine (partial reversion, lease and mortgage), about 7 on abolition, vesting, notice or pending proceedings, and 2 on a raiyati interest not merging.

**Recurring facts:** A landlord-tenant relationship or subordinate holding existed before the event said to end it.; The tenant or occupant acquired only some co-owners' or part of the landlord's interest, or held a lease and a mortgage in different capacities.; Abolition, vesting or acquisition of the landlord's estate was said to terminate existing tenancies.; A notice, a pending ejectment or possession application, or a superior-title suit was filed, but no final order ended the tenancy.; The party seeking a termination had an interest in asserting merger or extinction.

**Provisions:** Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss.105, 109, 111(d), 44, 58 and 101; Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1950, ss.32(2) and 44(1); Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act 1954, ss.3 and 33; Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act 1954, s.6(1); Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1948, ss.32, 32-O and 32G; Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act 1955, ss.4-9 and 28; Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act 1953, ss.9, 14-A and 18; Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1955, ss.4, 7 and 7A; Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act 1980, ss.4(1) and 4(2); Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1960, s.2(6)

**Exceptions/limits:** Merger does end a lease where the lessor's and lessee's interests in the whole property vest simultaneously in one person in the same right with no intervening or outstanding interest.; A subordinate interest can merge where a clear intention to merge is shown, apart from statute.; Where a statutory provision extinguishing the landlord-tenant relationship has come into force, or an eviction order or decree has been validly made before the relevant date, the relationship ends.; The conclusions depend on the particular statute in each case (for example the Transfer of Property Act s.111(d), the Hyderabad and Bombay tenancy and abolition statutes, and the Punjab, Pepsu and Tamil Nadu statutes) and should not be extended beyond the provisions considered.

**Split suggestion:** Split into (a) merger cases (108721012_1, 500624_1, 628977_2, 362062_1, 601351_1, 876929_2, 1578099_1, 1578099_2); (b) continuation of tenancy after abolition, vesting, acquisition, notice or pending proceedings (1126588_3, 1295163_1, 1295163_2, 1295956_1, 1338325_1, 32246_1, 628271_3, 739777_1); and (c) statutory limits on tenant protection or remedies (1295163_3, 1377832_3, 493375_1).

## 8.3 (19 issues)

**Question:** When does an amendment apply to proceedings that were pending when it took effect, or to claims and events that arose before it, rather than operating only prospectively?

**Rule:** IF `amendment_in_force_and_relevant_to_dispute and (transitional_or_express_provision_covers_the_proceeding or amendment_is_procedural_without_affecting_vested_substantive_rights or amendment_is_clarificatory_or_declaratory_of_existing_law or retrospective_intent_clearly_inferred_from_language_and_connected_provisions) and not exclusion_or_saving_for_the_proceeding_applies` THEN `amendment_applies_to_the_pending_or_earlier_arising_matter`

**Definition:** An amendment governs a pending proceeding, or a claim that arose before it, where the legislature has said so expressly or by transitional provision, where it is purely procedural, where it only clarifies existing law, or where retrospective intent is clearly implied. A substantive amendment without such indications operates only prospectively, although it can still apply to acts such as awards made after commencement in proceedings that began earlier.

- `amendment_in_force_and_relevant_to_dispute`: The amending provision has come into force and bears on the issue the court must decide in the proceeding or claim.
- `transitional_or_express_provision_covers_the_proceeding`: The amending Act, through a transitional clause, a retrospectivity or deeming clause, or a pending-proceedings clause, expressly extends the amendment to this kind of proceeding. It may do so by reference to a cut-off date or to the stage reached, for example whether an award had been made or the proceeding began after a given date.
- `amendment_is_procedural_without_affecting_vested_substantive_rights`: The amendment governs only procedure, evidence or method, such as the mode of recovery, valuation method or res judicata, and does not create, alter or take away substantive rights or liabilities.
- `amendment_is_clarificatory_or_declaratory_of_existing_law`: The amendment merely clarifies, declares or cures doubt or conflict about what the earlier law already meant, rather than changing it prejudicially.
- `retrospective_intent_clearly_inferred_from_language_and_connected_provisions`: Although retrospectivity is not stated for this provision, the language, context and linked provisions show unequivocally that the legislature intended it to operate retrospectively.
- `exclusion_or_saving_for_the_proceeding_applies`: The amending Act expressly excludes the provision from the general rule for pending proceedings, or contains a saving that protects this proceeding.
- `amendment_applies_to_the_pending_or_earlier_arising_matter`: The amended law governs the pending proceeding or the earlier-arising claim, or a later proceeding or award that relies on earlier facts, to the extent the amendment covers it.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 19/19 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 19 members the amendment was held to apply to the pending proceeding or earlier-arising claim, or to the later award or proceeding at issue. About 8 rest on transitional or express retrospective language, about 4 on the procedural character of the change, about 4 on a clarificatory or declaratory character, and 1 on inference from connected provisions. One member (1806862_3) applies the amendment only prospectively, but still allows it to operate on awards made after commencement in references pending at commencement.

**Recurring facts:** A proceeding (suit, appeal, acquisition, reference or assessment) was pending, or a claim had arisen, when the amending law took effect.; The amending Act contained a transitional clause, a pending-proceedings clause or a deeming-retrospectivity clause.; The amendment was described as procedural, evidentiary, clarificatory or declaratory.; In land acquisition cases, the Collector's or court's award date, the date possession was taken and a statutory cut-off date determined whether the benefit applied.

**Provisions:** Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 23(1-A), 28-A, 18 and 3(d); Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, Section 30(1)(a) and (b); Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act, 1976, Section 97(3); Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 48; Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966; Income Tax Act, 1961, Sections 22 and 27(iii), (iiia), (iiib); Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, Sections 1(3) and 2; Gujarat Amendment Act, 1965, Sections 7 and 18 (Sections 43C and 88(1)(b) of the tenancy law); Pre-emption law amendment of 1964 (Section 15(2)(b)) and Section 31 of the 1960 amendment; Tenure and land-reform amendment provisions, including Sections 4 and 7 and Sections 157(1)(a) and 21(h)

**Exceptions/limits:** A substantive provision that creates or alters rights is prospective unless the statutory language or necessary intendment shows retrospective intent, as for the redetermination remedy and the additional-amount provision.; An amendment that is prospective does not reopen concluded awards or decisions made before commencement. It can apply to a later award or decision made in a proceeding pending at commencement.; Transitional provisions apply only to the categories and cut-off dates they specify, for example proceedings pending on the bill's introduction with no Collector's award by then, or proceedings commenced after a stated date.; An express exclusion or saving for pending proceedings displaces the general rule that procedural amendments apply to them. Absent express words, no saving for pending litigation will be implied in an expressly retrospective amendment.; An express retrospective amendment is applied according to its plain terms, even if the legislature enacted it on a mistaken assumption about the law.

**Split suggestion:** The members share one theme, the temporal reach of amendments to pending or earlier matters. If a finer split is wanted, divide them into (a) the Land Acquisition Act Section 23(1-A) and Section 28-A transitional-provision members (1296921_3, 1698351_1, 1806862_3, 183116_1, 183116_2, 812937_3, 845127_1), (b) procedural-amendment members (1315480_1, 1401686_3, 1463870_2, 1842039_2), and (c) clarificatory or express-retrospectivity members (1338345_4, 147362898_4, 1658374_1, 21176_1, 242594_2, 289533_1, 518414_2, 82667_2).

## 11.3 (19 issues)

**Question:** Does an earlier proceeding that ended without a reasoned decision on the merits (a non-speaking or in limine dismissal, refusal of special leave, withdrawal, or dismissal for laches or alternative remedy) bar a later proceeding on the same matter through res judicata, merger or precedent?

**Rule:** IF `later_proceeding_raised and earlier_proceeding_ended_without_merits_determination and not earlier_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking_order and not earlier_findings_relevant_to_later_claim` THEN `earlier_disposal_does_not_bar_later_proceeding`

**Definition:** A prior disposal that did not decide the relevant issue on the merits by a reasoned order does not bar a later proceeding. This covers non-speaking or in limine dismissals, withdrawals, dismissals for laches or alternative remedy, and refusals of special leave. Such a disposal creates no res judicata, no merger of the challenged order, and no precedent. The later forum may still examine the matter, and review remains open.

- `later_proceeding_raised`: A later writ, suit, review, appeal or special leave proceeding has been brought on the same matter, or on a related issue, that was before an earlier forum.
- `earlier_proceeding_ended_without_merits_determination`: The earlier proceeding was dismissed in limine or by a non-speaking order, was withdrawn, was dismissed for laches or an available alternative remedy, or was a special leave petition refused without granting leave or giving reasons. It may also have been one in which the relevant issue was never raised or decided.
- `earlier_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking_order`: The earlier forum finally decided the relevant issue on the merits by a reasoned or speaking order.
- `earlier_findings_relevant_to_later_claim`: Facts found in the earlier proceeding are themselves relevant to the later claim.
- `earlier_disposal_does_not_bar_later_proceeding`: The earlier disposal does not operate as res judicata, merger, declared law or an otherwise binding bar, and the later proceeding may be considered on its merits.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 13/19 shown · outliers 6

**Typical outcome:** In all 13 covered members the earlier non-merits or non-speaking disposal was held not to bar the later proceeding. Eight of these concern special leave dismissals, and the remainder concern writ dismissals. Of the six outliers, five reject a procedural objection to maintainability and one (87147211_1) dismisses a writ because a first appeal was available.

**Recurring facts:** An earlier writ petition or special leave petition was dismissed in limine, by a non-speaking order, or by withdrawal.; A later suit, writ, review or appeal was then filed, and the opposing party pleaded res judicata, merger or an implied affirmation of the decision.; The earlier forum did not give reasons or decide the merits, or the later issue had not been raised earlier.

**Provisions:** Article 136 of the Constitution; Article 141 of the Constitution; Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution; Section 11 CPC; Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC; Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala (2000) 6 SCC 359; Daryao v. State of U.P.; Workmen of Cochin Port Trust v. Board of Trustees of the Cochin Port Trust

**Exceptions/limits:** A matter decided on the merits by a speaking order in an earlier writ or other proceeding may operate as res judicata.; Facts found by the earlier court may remain relevant and bind or influence the later proceeding, as in the laches and alternative-remedy dismissal context.; The Supreme Court's Article 136 jurisdiction is discretionary, so whether it entertains a later appeal can still depend on the circumstances, for example manifest injustice or case progress.; Where an effective statutory or appellate remedy is available and unused, the court may still dismiss a writ and leave that remedy open.

**Split suggestion:** Keep the 13 covered members as the core group on the preclusive effect of non-merits dismissals. This group could be split into (a) refusal of special leave (merger, precedent and review) and (b) writ dismissals (res judicata). Treat 1690960_2 and 707752_1 as a separate group on unpursued intermediate appeals before special leave. Treat 1407555_3, 87147211_1, 1459209_1 and 953085_2 as separate procedural and maintainability issues.

## 7.6 (18 issues)

**Question:** Does an entry in revenue, mutation, settlement or similar fiscal records (including occupancy entries, pattas and municipal tax entries) establish or transfer title to immovable property, or is it only evidence of possession or liability to pay revenue?

**Rule:** IF `title_to_immovable_property_in_dispute and claimant_relies_on_revenue_or_fiscal_record_entry_as_proof_of_title and not independent_title_established_by_valid_instrument_or_other_evidence` THEN `entry_does_not_establish_or_transfer_title_and_at_most_supports_rebuttable_inference_of_possession`

**Definition:** Revenue, mutation, settlement, patta and municipal tax entries are fiscal or administrative records; they do not create, transfer or extinguish title. They may support a rebuttable presumption of possession or show liability for revenue, but title must be proved by independent evidence.

- `title_to_immovable_property_in_dispute`: Ownership or title to land or other immovable property is contested in the proceeding.
- `claimant_relies_on_revenue_or_fiscal_record_entry_as_proof_of_title`: The claimant relies on a revenue record, mutation entry, record-of-rights entry, occupant entry, settlement patta, municipal tax entry or similar fiscal record as proof of ownership.
- `independent_title_established_by_valid_instrument_or_other_evidence`: The claimant has proved title through a valid transfer instrument, such as a registered deed, or other cogent evidence independent of the fiscal entry.
- `entry_does_not_establish_or_transfer_title_and_at_most_supports_rebuttable_inference_of_possession`: The entry neither creates, transfers nor extinguishes title and has no presumptive value as to title; it may at most support a rebuttable inference of possession or show who is liable for revenue or tax.

**Coherence:** high · covered 17/18 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In about 17 of 18 members the Court held that the entry did not establish or transfer title, usually allowing it as evidence of possession or revenue liability. One member (162171512_5) is an outlier. In most members the claim failed or the lower court's reliance on the entry was reversed.

**Recurring facts:** A party relies on a mutation, occupancy, record-of-rights, patta or tax entry to claim ownership.; No registered or valid transfer instrument, or no other independent evidence of title, was produced.; Entries were often made after the dispute arose or during pending litigation, or recorded only occupancy or possession.; Competing title, often the Government's, or an unproved gift, sale or heirship was in issue.

**Provisions:** Indian Evidence Act, 1872, ss. 35, 110 and 114; Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, ss. 3, 8, 11, 12, 43 and 46; Land Registration Act, 1876 (Register D); Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 6; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, s. 145; Indian Penal Code, 1860, ss. 154 and 158

**Exceptions/limits:** Revenue entries may carry evidentiary value, even strong prima facie value, and a rebuttable presumption of possession, but they are not conclusive of title.; Where there is no or very little proof of ownership, lawful possession may support a rebuttable presumption of title; this does not arise where the facts disclose a competing title.; Long-standing entries and tax payments may be considered with other evidence, and entries made after a dispute arose carry little weight.; Non-production of revenue records does not defeat title where the missing records do not affect title.; A statutory scheme may make a revenue authority's determination final on matters entrusted to it, but only within that scheme.

## 12.5 (18 issues)

**Question:** When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?

**Rule:** IF `rent_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_cured_or_met_payment_requirement_in_permitted_manner and not statute_makes_past_default_independently_sufficient and not independent_eviction_ground_established` THEN `tenant_not_evictable_for_rent_default`

**Definition:** Rent-control statutes protect a tenant from eviction for rent default where the tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears as the statute or court allows, or where the landlord's long unprotested acceptance of irregular payments shows there is no habitual or wilful default. The protection does not apply where the statute makes failure to pay within the notice period a complete ground for eviction, or where a separate eviction ground is established.

- `rent_default_eviction_proceeding`: The landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control or tenancy statute on a ground of non-payment, wilful default, habitual arrears or irregular payment of rent.
