- `rent_related_claim_or_ground_asserted`: A party asserts a claim for past rent, rent arrears, an eviction ground tied to rent default or tenant conduct, or reliance on a rent document.
- `tenancy_or_its_terms_or_rent_payable_not_established_by_evidence`: The party asserting the claim has not proved by evidence the tenancy, its terms, the rent rate or amount payable, or the facts alleged (for example, the rent document is too vague to identify the property or the parties, or the allegation of non-use is unsupported).
- `ground_not_pursued_on_appeal`: The ground relied on was rejected or not pursued or defended in the appellate proceedings, so it is not available to support the decree.
- `rent_related_claim_or_ground_fails`: The claim, ground or document is rejected or not accepted as establishing the relief or title sought.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** All six reject or confine the rent-based claim. Four concern unproved tenancy, rent or non-use; one concerns a vague rent note; one concerns a ground abandoned on appeal. The Supreme Court mostly leaves the lower findings undisturbed.

**Recurring facts:** Landlord or plaintiff asserts a tenancy, rent arrears or a rent default without adequate proof; Courts below or the High Court rejected the claim on evidence, and the Supreme Court declined to interfere; Key evidence is missing (rent rate, tenancy terms, identifying details, a witness with knowledge); Some grounds were not pursued in the appeal

**Provisions:** U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 and the preceding Ordinance (permission for letting); Section 13(1)(ff), West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956; Sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a), Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947

**Exceptions/limits:** Two members (1286314_2, and in part 1167532_2) also note that under the U.P. rent control legislation a letting without the required permission would be invalid; this is an additional, not a necessary, ground.; The appellate-abandonment strand (1601894_1, 860753_3) depends on the ground not having been pursued or defended on appeal and, in 1601894_1, on a statutory amendment changing the requirements.; The rule concerns failure of proof; it does not apply where the tenancy, its terms and the rent are proved.

**Split suggestion:** Split into (a) failure to prove tenancy, terms, rent or alleged facts (1167532_2, 1286314_2, 1593488_2, 61939581_10, and the non-use part of 860753_3) and (b) grounds not pursued or defended on appeal (1601894_1 and the default part of 860753_3).

## 136.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** When an eviction or ejectment decree has been passed and the occupant stays in possession after it (whether because of a stay pending appeal or delayed execution), must or may the court require payment of mesne profits or compensation for post-decree use and occupation, and is that compensation limited to the contractual rent?

**Rule:** IF `possession_decree_passed and occupant_remains_in_possession_after_decree and (possession_not_yet_delivered or execution_stayed_or_delayed)` THEN `occupant_liable_to_pay_reasonable_post_decree_compensation_for_use_and_occupation`

**Definition:** Once a decree for ejectment or eviction has been passed, an occupant who stays in possession must pay reasonable mesne profits or compensation for use and occupation from the decree until possession is delivered. A decree for ejectment should include such a direction. Where execution is stayed or delayed, the court may impose payment as a condition of the stay or as interim relief. The amount may reflect the market rent and is not capped at the contractual rent.

- `possession_decree_passed`: A court or tribunal has passed a decree or order for ejectment or eviction of the occupant, in favour of the landlord or claimant.
- `occupant_remains_in_possession_after_decree`: The occupant or tenant continues to hold the property after the decree has been passed.
- `possession_not_yet_delivered`: Possession has not yet been handed over to the decree-holder.
- `execution_stayed_or_delayed`: Execution of the decree is stayed pending appeal or is otherwise delayed, so the decree-holder is kept out of possession.
- `occupant_liable_to_pay_reasonable_post_decree_compensation_for_use_and_occupation`: The court may (and in a plain ejectment decree must) direct the occupant to pay reasonable mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the decree until possession is delivered. The amount may reflect the market rent and is not capped at the contractual rent.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All six members award or uphold post-decree compensation for use and occupation. Two (1167532_3, 1286314_3) hold that the ejectment decree must include future mesne profits. Four (1452318_2, 1651002_1, 309033_1, 77210495_3) allow compensation to be imposed during a stay or delay, in three of them at market-based rates exceeding the contractual rent.

**Recurring facts:** A decree or order for ejectment or eviction had been passed in favour of the landlord or claimant.; The occupant or tenant remained in possession after the decree.; Execution was stayed pending appeal or otherwise delayed in four members.; The contractual rent was low compared with the market rent in the stay cases, and the landlord sought compensation for the delay.

**Provisions:** Order XLI Rule 5 and Rule 5(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure; Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure; Section 38(3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958; Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd.; Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd.; State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd.; South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P.; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation

**Exceptions/limits:** The obligation is mandatory only where the decree for ejectment is itself being granted or finalised (two members); during a stay or delay the members describe it as discretionary, as reasonable terms imposed by the court.; The compensation must be reasonable. In one member the tenant did not contend that the amount was grossly excessive.; A stay is discretionary and equitable, not a right, and Order 41 Rule 5(3) considerations (substantial loss, delay, security) apply.; The interim-compensation order in the delayed-execution member did not decide the merits of the occupant's claimed tenancy rights, which were pending in a separate suit.

## 34.5 (6 issues)

**Question:** Can a court or revenue/execution sale be set aside merely because the price obtained was allegedly inadequate, without proof of fraud or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale causing substantial injury?

**Rule:** IF `compulsory_sale_challenged and inadequate_price_alleged and not (fraud_or_material_irregularity_in_sale_proved and substantial_injury_shown)` THEN `sale_not_set_aside_for_price_inadequacy_alone`

**Definition:** A compulsory court or revenue sale is not liable to be set aside or declared void merely because the price was allegedly inadequate. The challenger must prove fraud or a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale, together with substantial injury caused by it (Order XXI Rule 90 CPC), and must also offer evidence of the higher value claimed.

- `compulsory_sale_challenged`: The challenge is to a sale held in execution of a court decree or as a revenue sale, i.e. a compulsory sale rather than a private sale.
- `inadequate_price_alleged`: The challenger alleges that the property fetched less than its true or estimated value.
- `fraud_or_material_irregularity_in_sale_proved`: The challenger has proved fraud, or a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
- `substantial_injury_shown`: The challenger has shown that the fraud or irregularity caused substantial injury.
- `sale_not_set_aside_for_price_inadequacy_alone`: The sale is not set aside or declared void on the ground of alleged inadequacy of price alone.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 6 members, inadequacy of price alone did not justify setting aside the sale. In 1362442_11 the sale was nonetheless set aside on other grounds, and in 155745050_2 the executing court's dismissal of the objection was restored.

**Recurring facts:** The judgment-debtor or owner alleges that the property was sold for far less than its worth.; No fraud or material irregularity in publication or conduct of the sale was alleged or proved.; There was no reliable evidence that the property was worth substantially more.; The sale was a court execution or auction sale, or a revenue sale.

**Provisions:** Order XXI Rule 90 CPC (fraud or material irregularity plus substantial injury); Section 47 CPC; Order XXI Rules 54, 64, 66-68 CPC (proclamation and sale procedure); Kayjay Industries v. Asnew Drums (court sale is a forced sale); Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin

**Exceptions/limits:** The sale can still be set aside on independent grounds, such as procedural defects, excessive execution, or proven fraud or material irregularity causing substantial injury (as in 1362442_11).; Inadequacy of price may be relevant evidence where it is tied to proven irregularity or fraud, but it does not suffice by itself.; The challenger bears the burden of proving the higher value, fraud or irregularity, and substantial injury; bare assertions do not suffice.; A challenge brought as an objection under section 47 CPC rather than under Order XXI Rule 90 does not widen the available grounds (1190054_2).

## 126.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Can the government or a superior executive authority direct a statutory authority (a Collector or development authority) to take a particular action in respect of land that the governing statute commits to that authority, where the direction is unauthorised, bypasses the prescribed procedure, or conflicts with the statute's purposes?

**Rule:** IF `statutory_authority_vested_with_power_over_land and government_or_superior_authority_directs_specific_action_on_that_land and (direction_not_authorized_by_statute or direction_conflicts_with_statutory_purpose_or_scheme or prescribed_statutory_procedure_bypassed)` THEN `direction_and_resulting_action_invalid_and_not_binding`

**Definition:** A statutory power over land must be exercised by the authority named in the statute, in the prescribed manner and for the statute's purposes. A government direction that is unauthorised, bypasses the prescribed procedure or runs contrary to the statute's purposes is not binding, and action taken under it is invalid. General supervisory or direction powers do not let the government usurp the authority's function.

- `statutory_authority_vested_with_power_over_land`: The governing statute or rules assign the decision on transfer, allotment, disposal or reconveyance of the land to a designated statutory authority such as a Collector or development authority.
- `government_or_superior_authority_directs_specific_action_on_that_land`: The State Government, a Minister or another superior executive authority directs the statutory authority to take a particular action on an individual matter concerning the land.
- `direction_not_authorized_by_statute`: No provision of the statute, rules or the Constitution (including a valid government order under Article 166) authorises the direction, or the general supervisory or direction power relied on does not extend to individual matters.
- `direction_conflicts_with_statutory_purpose_or_scheme`: The directed action is contrary to the purposes of the Act, the development scheme, or the specific conditions and rules governing the power.
- `prescribed_statutory_procedure_bypassed`: The statutory inquiry, process or conditions prescribed for exercising the power were not followed.
- `direction_and_resulting_action_invalid_and_not_binding`: The direction does not bind the statutory authority, and any permission, allotment or transfer made under it is invalid and liable to be set aside.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In 5 of 6 members the government direction and the resulting permission, allotment or transfer were held invalid or not binding. The sixth held that a development authority cannot be compelled to reconvey land because it has no statutory power to do so.

**Recurring facts:** Land is vested in, or its disposal is entrusted by statute to, a Collector or development authority.; The State Government, a Minister or the Chief Minister directs a particular transfer, allotment, reconveyance or conversion of the land.; The directed action departs from the statutory scheme, such as an open space or civic amenity site, the prescribed process or the authority's own rules.; The authority often implemented the direction without exercising its own independent judgment.

**Provisions:** Sections 89, 89A and 126 of the Tenancy Act; Sections 15(3), 19(4), 32(5), 38-A and 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976; Article 166 of the Constitution; Sections 58, 72 and 73 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, and Rules 3–5 and 19–20 of the 1975 Rules; Section 29(2) of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945

**Exceptions/limits:** Government directions are valid where the statute authorises them and they are necessary or expedient for carrying out the Act's purposes (e.g. Section 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act).; Where the statute requires prior State approval for disposal, the State may exercise that approval role, but it cannot itself take over the disposal function.; The reconveyance issue rests on the absence of any statutory power to reconvey; it does not turn on a government direction.

**Split suggestion:** Keep the five members on invalid government directions to statutory authorities together. Treat 1271427_1 (no statutory power to reconvey acquired land) as a separate issue on the limits of a development authority's statutory powers, or pair it with 1271427_5, which arises from the same case.

## 34.4 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a statutory provision barring courts from questioning orders made under the Act (or excluding civil suits) prevent a court from examining an order that was made without jurisdiction, outside the statute, or in breach of fundamental procedure or natural justice?

**Rule:** IF `challenge_to_statutory_order_protected_by_bar and (order_made_without_essential_jurisdictional_prerequisite or order_outside_statutory_scope_or_authority or order_in_breach_of_fundamental_procedure_or_natural_justice) and not authority_properly_exercised_jurisdiction` THEN `statutory_bar_does_not_oust_court_review`

**Definition:** A clause barring court challenges protects only orders validly made within the authority's jurisdiction and procedure. Courts may still examine, and set aside, orders made without a jurisdictional prerequisite, outside the statute, or in breach of fundamental procedure or natural justice. They cannot review the propriety of orders made in the proper exercise of jurisdiction.

- `challenge_to_statutory_order_protected_by_bar`: A court challenge is brought against an order or action under a statute that contains a clause barring or excluding court challenges or civil suits.
- `order_made_without_essential_jurisdictional_prerequisite`: The authority made the order without a jurisdictional fact or statutory prerequisite on which its power depended (for example a prior requisition or an actual vacancy).
- `order_outside_statutory_scope_or_authority`: The order or action falls outside the statute or beyond the limited authority conferred on the tribunal or officer, so it is a nullity for jurisdictional error.
- `order_in_breach_of_fundamental_procedure_or_natural_justice`: The order was made in violation of fundamental principles of judicial procedure, without relevant evidence, without reasonable opportunity to be heard, or without vital procedural requirements.
- `authority_properly_exercised_jurisdiction`: The authority acted within its jurisdiction and followed the required procedure, so only the correctness or propriety of the order is in question.
- `statutory_bar_does_not_oust_court_review`: The statutory bar does not prevent the court from entertaining the challenge and examining the order, which may be set aside or quashed.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 6 members the statutory bar was held not to prevent court examination of the challenged order, in 5 because of a jurisdictional defect, outside-statute action or procedural violation, and in 1 because the Government was a formal party. Two members also limit review: no review of propriety where jurisdiction was properly exercised, and a preference for statutory remedies in demolition cases.

**Recurring facts:** A statute contained a clause barring court challenges to orders made under it, or barring civil suits.; The challenge alleged that the authority lacked a jurisdictional prerequisite (requisition, vacancy), acted outside the statute, or violated procedure or natural justice.; Several cases involved rent control, allotment, rent-fixing or land acquisition orders.

**Provisions:** Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, ss. 3, 4, 11; U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, ss. 7, 7A, 16; Section 8(1) and s. 3(2) of the rent-fixing statute; Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, s. 4(a); Code of Civil Procedure, s. 9; Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, ss. 343(4)-(5), 347E

**Exceptions/limits:** Where the authority properly exercised its jurisdiction, the court cannot examine the propriety or merits of the order.; Where a statute provides appellate remedies, the court ordinarily directs the aggrieved person to them, and entertains a suit only if the order is prima facie a nullity, outside the statute, or vital procedures were not followed (demolition context).; Where a statutory bar concerns claims against the Government, it does not apply if the Government is only a formal party and no substantive relief is sought against it; it does apply where the claim cannot be separated from relief against the Government.; Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction is not readily inferred.

## 137.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Is a lease granted during the subsistence of a mortgage, whether by the mortgagor in possession or by the mortgagee in possession, binding on the other party to the mortgage, on the redeeming owner, or on an auction-purchaser, and does it bind only if made in the ordinary or prudent course of management, as strictly proved by the party relying on it?

**Rule:** IF `mortgage_lease_dispute and lease_granted_by_party_in_possession_under_mortgage and not lease_proved_to_be_ordinary_prudent_management_by_party_relying_on_it` THEN `lease_does_not_bind_the_other_mortgage_party_or_successor`

**Definition:** A lease made by a mortgagor in possession (under the pre-section 65-A law) or by a mortgagee in possession binds the other party, the redeeming mortgagor or an auction-purchaser only if it was a bona fide act of ordinary, prudent management. The party relying on the lease must strictly prove this. Otherwise the lease ends with the grantor's interest and does not bind them.

- `mortgage_lease_dispute`: The dispute concerns whether a lease created while a mortgage subsisted binds the mortgagee, the mortgagor after redemption, or a purchaser who acquired their interest.
- `lease_granted_by_party_in_possession_under_mortgage`: The lease was granted during the mortgage by the mortgagor in possession (under the pre-section 65-A law) or by the mortgagee in possession.
- `lease_proved_to_be_ordinary_prudent_management_by_party_relying_on_it`: The party relying on the lease has established, with strict proof, that it was made on usual terms in the ordinary course of management, or as a prudent owner would manage the property (section 76(a) for mortgagee leases).
- `lease_does_not_bind_the_other_mortgage_party_or_successor`: The lease is not binding on the mortgagee, the mortgagor after redemption, or the successor or auction-purchaser who acquired the relevant interest, and the lease ends with the grantor's interest.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In all 6 members the lease was held not binding on the mortgagee, successor, purchaser or redeeming mortgagor, or at most binding temporarily without occupancy rights (1606165_4). The strict burden on the lessee to prove prudent management was decisive in 5 of the 6.

**Recurring facts:** A lease was granted by a mortgagor in possession or a mortgagee in possession while the mortgage subsisted.; The mortgage was later redeemed or enforced, or the property was sold in execution, and the owner, successor or purchaser sought possession against the lessees.; The lessee or tenant failed to prove usual terms or prudent management, or the courts found the lease imprudent or in bad faith.; Leases were long-term, permanent or low-rent, or changed the character of the land.

**Provisions:** Transfer of Property Act 1882, s. 76(a) (mortgagee in possession must manage as a person of ordinary prudence); Transfer of Property Act 1882, s. 65-A (inserted 1929; not applicable to earlier mortgages); Transfer of Property Act 1882, s. 66 (waste; held not to govern the power to lease); Transfer of Property Act 1882, s. 111(c) (lease determines when the lessor's interest ends); Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh [1952] S.C.R. 775; Asaram v. Ram Kali [1958] S.C.R. 986

**Exceptions/limits:** Where the lease is proved to be an ordinary and prudent act of management, it may bind the mortgagee, mortgagor or successor, but only for its applicable duration. It does not confer permanent or occupancy rights (1606165_4).; For mortgagor leases, the rule applies to leases under mortgages governed by the law before section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act (inserted in 1929). Later mortgages fall under the statutory leasing power.; A successor who adopts or recreates the tenancy, or a mortgagor who expressly consents to its continuance beyond the mortgage, may be bound (1274804_1).; The absence of a prohibition on leasing in the mortgage deed does not by itself make the lease binding (387828_1).

**Split suggestion:** Optionally split into (a) mortgagor-in-possession leases binding the mortgagee or auction-purchaser under the pre-1929 law (1251841_1, 140352_2), (b) mortgagee-in-possession leases binding the mortgagor after redemption under s. 76(a) (1274804_1, 1348467_2, 387828_1), and (c) the duration and occupancy-right consequences of a protected lease (1606165_4).

## 124.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Can the State take or retain possession of private property, or evict occupants, by executive action without following a procedure authorised by law, and what follows when it does so?

**Rule:** IF `state_took_or_seeks_possession_of_property and no_lawful_authority_or_prescribed_process_followed and (owner_or_occupant_entitled_to_protection)` THEN `state_action_is_unlawful_and_possession_must_be_obtained_through_law_with_compensation_where_property_is_taken`

**Definition:** The State cannot deprive a person of property or possession except by authority of law and a legally prescribed procedure. A general power to secure possession, a public-purpose claim, or an enforcement power meant for other persons or processes does not justify self-help or forcible eviction. Where property was taken without lawful process, the owner is entitled to lawful acquisition and compensation.

- `state_took_or_seeks_possession_of_property`: The State or government has taken, retained, or is trying to obtain possession of private property or premises from an owner or occupant.
- `no_lawful_authority_or_prescribed_process_followed`: The possession was taken or sought by executive action, force, or by invoking a power that does not apply to the person or situation, without a legally prescribed acquisition, eviction or possession procedure.
- `owner_or_occupant_entitled_to_protection`: The affected person is an owner whose title is admitted or not disputed by the State, or an occupant (such as a continuing tenant) whom the invoked power does not cover.
- `state_action_is_unlawful_and_possession_must_be_obtained_through_law_with_compensation_where_property_is_taken`: The State's taking, retention or forcible eviction is impermissible; it must proceed through a procedure recognised by law, and the owner must be compensated where property was taken without such process.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 6 members hold the State's action unlawful. Two (the road-taking and the retained-possession cases) direct compensation or lawful acquisition. Four (the hotel-acquisition issues) hold that possession must be obtained in due course of law and that the invoked power or justification does not authorise forcible eviction.

**Recurring facts:** The State took or kept possession of property by executive action, without acquisition proceedings or a lawful possession process.; The State relied on a statutory power or a public-interest justification that did not fit the situation.; The owner or occupant remained entitled to protection, through admitted title or continuing tenancy.

**Provisions:** Article 300A and former Article 31 of the Constitution; Section 4(8) of the Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1980; Section 6A of the West Bengal Government Premises (Tenancy Regulation) Act, 1976; Section 47 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894

**Exceptions/limits:** The rule does not bar the State from acquiring or recovering possession through a procedure that is authorised by law and followed.; A statutory force power applies only to the class of persons it names, for example non-tenants without written authority. It cannot be used against tenants or others outside that class.; The compensation consequence is stated only for the unlawful-taking and owner-title-conceded members. The eviction members require possession to be obtained in due course of law, without a separate compensation ruling.; The Court did not decide whether the 1976 West Bengal Act applies only to residential premises.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally split into (a) uncompensated taking or retention of land without acquisition under Article 300A (127924004_1, 46771491_2) and (b) limits on statutory possession, enforcement and eviction powers (1338325_2, 1338325_3, 1338325_4, 1338325_6).

## 33.5 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a final decision on the merits by a competent court or tribunal, including in a constitutional writ proceeding or quasi-judicial proceeding that is not itself a suit, bar the same parties or their privies from relitigating the same issue or matter in a later proceeding?

**Rule:** IF `prior_competent_forum_decision_on_merits and prior_decision_final_not_reversed_or_modified and same_parties_or_privies and same_issue_or_matter_directly_decided and later_proceeding_seeks_to_relitigate` THEN `later_proceeding_barred_by_res_judicata`

**Definition:** Res judicata rests on public policy and finality and is not confined to the technical terms of Section 11 CPC. A final merits decision of a competent court, writ court or quasi-judicial tribunal binds the same parties or their privies on the same issue in later proceedings, unless it has been reversed or modified through an appropriate remedy.

- `prior_competent_forum_decision_on_merits`: An earlier proceeding (a suit, a writ petition under Article 32 or 226, or a quasi-judicial tribunal proceeding) was decided on the merits by a forum with jurisdiction, after a contest or a fair opportunity to contest.
- `prior_decision_final_not_reversed_or_modified`: The earlier decision has attained finality and has not been reversed or modified through an appropriate appeal, review or constitutional remedy.
- `same_parties_or_privies`: The later proceeding is between the same parties as the earlier one, or between persons claiming under them (privies).
- `same_issue_or_matter_directly_decided`: The issue or matter raised in the later proceeding is the same as one directly and substantially decided in the earlier proceeding (the same facts and the same or similar relief, where relief is relevant).
- `later_proceeding_seeks_to_relitigate`: The later suit or petition seeks to reopen or re-agitate the issue or matter already decided.
- `later_proceeding_barred_by_res_judicata`: The later suit or petition is barred, or the decided issue cannot be reopened, under Section 11 CPC or the general principle of res judicata.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 6 members, the later suit or petition was barred by res judicata or by a principle analogous to it. Of these, 4 involve earlier writ or constitutional proceedings, 1 an earlier civil suit, and 1 a quasi-judicial tribunal decision.

**Recurring facts:** An earlier proceeding (writ petition, suit, constitutional proceeding between States, or quasi-judicial application) was contested and decided on the merits.; A later suit or petition between the same parties raised the same issue, facts or relief.; The earlier decision was final: appeal confirmed, review dismissed, or not reversed or modified.

**Provisions:** Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (including Explanation VIII), treated as non-exhaustive; Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India; Daryao v. State of U.P.; Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha; Raj Lakshmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen

**Exceptions/limits:** The earlier forum must have been competent; a judgment of a court lacking inherent jurisdiction is a nullity and creates no bar.; The earlier decision must be on the merits, after a contest or fair opportunity to prove the case, and final; a decision reversed or modified through an appropriate procedure does not bar.; The parties (or privies) and the issue or matter must be the same.; A final finding may be reconsidered by the Court itself in changed circumstances, but cannot be unilaterally displaced by a legislature (as stated in the dam safety member).

## 40.2 (6 issues)

**Question:** On an application to reject a plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (no cause of action, or suit barred by law), what material may the court consider, and does it decide the application on the plaint alone, without the defendant's written statement, defence or evidence?

**Rule:** IF `application_to_reject_plaint and (cause_of_action_ground or apparent_legal_bar_ground)` THEN `court_decides_application_on_plaint_averments_read_as_a_whole_with_plaintiffs_documents_and_not_on_defence_or_outside_evidence`

**Definition:** When a plaint is challenged under Order VII Rule 11(a) or (d), the court must decide the application from the plaint's averments, read meaningfully and as a whole, together with the documents the plaintiff relies on. The defendant's written statement, disputed merits and evidence outside the plaint are irrelevant, and the application should be decided before the defendant is required to file a written statement. The power may be exercised at any stage before the trial concludes.

- `application_to_reject_plaint`: A party has applied under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint.
- `cause_of_action_ground`: The application asserts that the plaint discloses no cause of action.
- `apparent_legal_bar_ground`: The application asserts that the suit appears from the plaint's statements to be barred by law, for example by limitation.
- `court_decides_application_on_plaint_averments_read_as_a_whole_with_plaintiffs_documents_and_not_on_defence_or_outside_evidence`: The court decides the application only on the plaint's averments, assumed true and read as a whole, together with documents the plaintiff filed with and relied on in the plaint, and disregards the written statement, the defendant's pleas and evidence recorded outside the plaint. It does not defer the decision until the written statement is filed.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all six members the application is decided on the plaint alone. In about four, the court corrects a departure from that approach (a direction to file a written statement first, reliance on cross-examination, a part-wise reading, or reliance on defence material). One affirms rejection based on the plaint and its sale deed. One affirms a remittal after defence material was relied on.

**Recurring facts:** A defendant or owner applied under Order VII Rule 11 on the grounds of no cause of action and/or a legal bar such as limitation.; The defendant's written statement, defence pleas or evidence outside the plaint was invoked or relied upon by a court or party.; The courts below sometimes erred by looking beyond the plaint, by delaying the decision until the written statement was filed, or by reading the plaint in parts.

**Provisions:** Code of Civil Procedure, Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d); Order VII Rule 14(1); Order VI Rule 2; Order VI Rule 16

**Exceptions/limits:** Documents filed with and relied on by the plaintiff as the basis of the plaint (Order VII Rule 14) may be considered as part of the plaint.; The plaint's factual allegations are taken as true, but a sham or illusory cause of action created by clever drafting may still be rejected.; Rejection applies to the plaint as a whole; Order VII Rule 11 does not permit rejecting only part of a plaint or particular reliefs. Improper matter is dealt with under Order VI Rule 16.; Where the plaint as a whole discloses a cause of action and shows no legal bar, the application must be dismissed; where it discloses none or shows a bar, rejection is mandatory.; The decision cannot depend on evidence led in the trial, such as cross-examination answers.

## 125.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a statutory power to prohibit, restrict or control exports include the power to canalise export trade through selected agencies and exclude other participants, and is such canalisation, with a preference for a state trading agency and exclusion of new entrants, a reasonable restriction on the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) and 19(6)?

**Rule:** IF `export_control_case and government_has_statutory_power_to_control_exports and export_trade_is_channelled_through_selected_agencies` THEN `canalisation_and_resulting_exclusion_of_other_participants_is_within_statutory_power_and_not_an_unreasonable_restriction`

**Definition:** A power to control exports includes the power to canalise exports through selected agencies and to classify and limit who may export. Excluding newcomers and preferring a suitable state agency is a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6) where it has a rational basis in the nature of the trade and public export objectives such as regular, uniform-quality supply and foreign-exchange earnings.

- `export_control_case`: The dispute challenges an export restriction or licensing scheme made under export-control legislation or a delegated order.
- `government_has_statutory_power_to_control_exports`: The governing statute empowers the government to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control exports, and the order permits licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
- `export_trade_is_channelled_through_selected_agencies`: Exports of the commodity are routed through selected agencies or classes of exporters (for example, a state trading corporation and established exporters), so that other persons, such as newcomers, are excluded from direct export.
- `canalisation_and_resulting_exclusion_of_other_participants_is_within_statutory_power_and_not_an_unreasonable_restriction`: The canalisation provision is within the delegated rule-making power, and the exclusion of some participants is a permissible reasonable restriction in the public interest, provided it rests on a rational basis.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All six members uphold the scheme. Three (1405373_1, 247451_1, 29862148_1) hold that canalisation is within the statutory power. Three (1405373_2, 247451_2, 29862148_2) hold that exclusion of newcomers and preference for the state trading corporation is not an unreasonable restriction. 247451_2 carried a dissent.

**Recurring facts:** Manganese ore exports controlled through quotas and selected categories of exporters under an export control order; Order allowed licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies; Negligible domestic market, with the ore produced mainly for export; Newcomers without export performance in specified earlier years were excluded and could sell only to established exporters or the state trading corporation; Government aimed at regular supplies of uniform quality, continuity of trade and foreign-exchange earnings; The appellant did not allege that established exporters were improperly included

**Provisions:** Section 3, Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947; Clause 6(h), Export Control Order, 1958; Article 19(1)(g); Article 19(6) (first part) and 19(6)(ii); Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India; Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (referred to)

**Exceptions/limits:** The reasonableness holding depends on a rational basis for the classification and selection, for example a negligible domestic market, a need for reliable and uniform supply, and an agency suited to those objectives.; Exclusion alone does not show an unlawful restriction, but the challenger may succeed by showing improper inclusion of comparable participants or that the selected agency is unsuitable; none of the members found this shown.; Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorise a state monopoly by administrative action; the restriction must be justified under the general reasonable-restrictions limb.; The reasonableness holding was by majority; Subba Rao J. dissented in one member, finding the effects on excluded mine owners unreasonable.; A selected agency need not have prior expertise in the trade; it is 'special' because it is selected to advance the canalisation purpose.

## 138.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does property that has the character of Hindu joint-family property lose that character, and become the separate property of one member, merely because the coparcenary is reduced to a sole coparcener or the family status is severed, while the property remains unpartitioned and other family members (such as widows or daughters) have continuing rights?

**Rule:** IF `joint_family_property_character_dispute and property_was_joint_family_property and (only_one_coparcener_remains or family_status_severed_without_partition or sole_coparcener_received_property_on_partition) and not property_validly_partitioned_or_separately_acquired` THEN `property_retains_joint_family_character`

**Definition:** Joint-family property does not become the separate property of a single member merely because the coparcenary shrinks to one coparcener or because family status is severed. It retains joint-family character until it is actually partitioned, with the rights of widows, wives, daughters and possible future sons remaining relevant.

- `joint_family_property_character_dispute`: The case turns on whether certain property is joint-family property or the separate property of an individual member.
- `property_was_joint_family_property`: The property was impressed with joint-family (ancestral or coparcenary) character before the event relied on to change its character.
- `only_one_coparcener_remains`: Through death or partition, the coparcenary has been reduced to a single male coparcener, with female family members (widow, wife or daughters) still part of or having rights in the family.
- `family_status_severed_without_partition`: A member has declared an intention to sever the joint status, but the property has not been divided by metes and bounds.
- `sole_coparcener_received_property_on_partition`: A coparcener received joint-family property on partition and has no son or other male coparcener, though he has a wife or daughters.
- `not_property_validly_partitioned_or_separately_acquired`: Placeholder; see next entry.
- `property_validly_partitioned_or_separately_acquired`: The property has actually been partitioned among the members, or was the separate property of the holder before it came to him, rather than property already impressed with joint-family character.
- `property_retains_joint_family_character`: The property remains joint-family property (and the family may be assessed or treated as a joint family) and is not the individual property of the sole or severing member.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In all 5 covered members the property retained its joint-family character: 3 sole-coparcener cases after a death, 1 sole coparcener after partition, 1 severance without partition. The sixth member is an outlier on widow's maintenance.

**Recurring facts:** Ancestral or joint-family property held by brothers or a father and sons; One coparcener died or the coparcenary was reduced to a sole survivor; A widow, wife or daughters remained in the family, often with a maintenance right; A claim that the property had become the sole coparcener's or a member's personal property

**Provisions:** Wealth Tax Act 1957, sections 3 and 5(1)(ii); Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act 1956, section 19 (held not to govern in the outlier); Hindu Women's Right to Property Act 1937, section 3(2) (outlier); Gowli Buddanna v. CIT, Mysore; Attorney General of Ceylon v. A.R. Arunachalam Chettiar

**Exceptions/limits:** Does not apply to property that was the separate property of the holder before it came to him, rather than already impressed with joint-family character.; Does not apply once the property has been actually partitioned among the members.; The maintenance right of a widow of a predeceased son against the father-in-law's estate is a distinct point and does not itself decide the character of the property; it lasts only while she does not remarry.

**Split suggestion:** Treat 1849559_1 (a widow's maintenance right against a father-in-law's estate) as a separate cluster. Keep the other five together as the joint-family-character group.

## 127.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Under Section 3(2)(d) and Explanation (1) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, when is an inam grant of, or relating to, a village an 'estate', and does a grant expressed to be of a named village raise a presumption of estate status, and on whom lies the burden of proving or rebutting it where parts of the village were excluded or separately granted?

**Rule:** IF `inam_estate_classification_case and ((grant_expressed_as_named_village and not party_denying_estate_proved_exclusion_exception) or (grant_of_entire_village_proved and government_confirmed_or_recognised_whole_grant))` THEN `land_is_an_estate_under_section_3_2_d`

**Definition:** An inam village is an estate only if the grant was of the whole village (or expressed as a grant of a named village, which Explanation (1) allows despite excluded lands). Most members hold that a named-village grant raises a rebuttable presumption of estate status, with the burden on the party denying it. One member holds that the Explanation creates no presumption either way, and where the grant was shown to be of less than the whole village, estate status fails.

- `inam_estate_classification_case`: The dispute turns on whether land held under an inam grant is an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908 (including for rent reduction or occupancy rights consequences).
- `grant_expressed_as_named_village`: The grant, as shown by the available records, is expressed to be a grant of a named village.
- `party_denying_estate_proved_exclusion_exception`: The party contending that the land is not an estate has proved the facts taking the grant outside the definition, for example that the excluded minor inams were created by the grantor contemporaneously with or after the village grant and are not within the stated categories.
- `grant_of_entire_village_proved`: The evidence establishes that the grant covered the entire village and not merely a substantial part of it.
- `government_confirmed_or_recognised_whole_grant`: The Government made, confirmed or recognised the grant as extending to the whole village and not to only part of its area.
- `land_is_an_estate_under_section_3_2_d`: The land or village in question is held to be an 'estate' within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, so that the consequential legislation (such as rent reduction or estate abolition) applies to it.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** Estate status was upheld in 3 members (1435737_1, 872053_2, 703197_1). It was denied in 2 (1431341_1, 795303_3) because the grant was not shown to cover the whole village. 1479218_2 held that a named-village grant raises no presumption.

**Recurring facts:** The original grant deed was unavailable, so the grant's scope was inferred from inam registers and other records.; Minor inams or excluded lands existed within the village, and there was no evidence of when they were created or whether the grantor carved them out.; The dispute arose in the context of rent reduction, occupancy rights or abolition-related estate status.

**Provisions:** Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, s. 3(2)(d) and Explanation (1); Explanation (1-A), inserted by Act XXXV of 1956; Act 2 of 1945, which added the Explanation and applied it from the 1936 amendment; Madras Estates Rent Reduction Act, 1947

**Exceptions/limits:** The members conflict on whether a named-village grant raises a presumption. 1435737_1 and 872053_2 say it does, with the burden on the challenger. 1479218_2 says the Explanation creates no presumption either way, so the description alone does not establish the excluded lands' prior grant.; Where the claimant must prove estate status and the evidence shows only a substantial part of the village was granted, with no proof the grant was expressed as a named village or that the excluded lands were previously granted or reserved, the land is not an estate (1431341_1).; Where the grant was of less than the entire village and the Government confirmed only part of the area, with the excluded lands treated as separate property, the land is not an estate (795303_3).; Minor inams of immemorial or earlier origin, or created by the grantees, do not show reservation by the grantor and do not defeat estate status (703197_1).; The Explanation operates only if the grant is shown to be of a named village; Explanation (1-A) (1956) confirms that differing confirmation dates, title deeds or grantees do not defeat estate status.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally split into (a) the presumption/burden question for named-village grants (1435737_1, 872053_2, 1479218_2) and (b) the fact-based question of whether the grant covered the whole village and was confirmed as such (1431341_1, 795303_3, 703197_1).

## 139.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, is a landlord's eviction suit that requires official permission maintainable, depending on whether the permission was effective when the suit was instituted (or the decree passed) or was revoked or cancelled before or after institution?

**Rule:** IF `eviction_suit_requiring_permission and not permission_cancelled_or_revoked_before_filing and (permission_effective_at_institution or restored_permission_effective_before_decree)` THEN `suit_is_maintainable_and_later_revocation_does_not_defeat_it`

**Definition:** An eviction suit needing statutory permission is maintainable if valid permission existed when it was instituted. A later State Government revocation does not defeat it, because the revisional power is exhausted once the suit is validly instituted. A cancellation or revocation made before filing leaves no valid permission, and the suit is not maintainable. Where the Government sets aside a revocation, the restored permission supports the suit if it is effective when the decree is passed.

- `eviction_suit_requiring_permission`: The landlord's eviction suit falls in a category for which the statute requires prior official permission to sue.
- `permission_cancelled_or_revoked_before_filing`: The Commissioner or the State Government actually cancelled or revoked the permission before the suit was instituted, leaving no effective permission at filing.
- `permission_effective_at_institution`: A valid permission was in force when the suit was filed, so the suit was validly instituted.
- `restored_permission_effective_before_decree`: The original permission, after being revoked, was restored by the State Government setting aside the revocation, and it was effective when the decree was passed.
- `suit_is_maintainable_and_later_revocation_does_not_defeat_it`: The suit is maintainable, and a later revocation by the State Government does not make it incompetent or the decree unenforceable.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In the 5 covered members, a revocation after valid institution does not defeat the suit (3: 404039_3, 80590_1, and 1472953_1 where permission was restored and effective before decree). A cancellation or revocation before institution leaves the suit without valid permission (2: 404039_1, 404039_2).

**Recurring facts:** Landlord needs permission from the District Magistrate, the Commissioner or the State Government before suing for eviction.; Permission was granted, often by the Commissioner on revision, and the tenant sought revision or revocation before the State Government.; The timing of the revocation or cancellation relative to the filing of the suit and the passing of the decree is decisive.; A decree was often passed before the State Government's revocation order.

**Provisions:** U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, sections 3(1), 3(3), 3(4), 7-F and 14; Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, section 11A (outlier only)

**Exceptions/limits:** If the Commissioner cancels or the State Government revokes permission before the suit is instituted, the suit lacks valid permission and is not maintainable (404039_1, 404039_2).; The protection applies only to suits validly instituted under permission; a mere pending application for revocation before filing does not by itself defeat the suit, since the actual revocation came only after filing.; Where the Government directs that restored permission takes effect later, maintainability depends on its being effective when the decree is passed (1472953_1).; The rule rests on the absence of statutory language making a validly instituted suit incompetent or a decree inexecutable; it does not cover express statutory provisions to the contrary.

**Split suggestion:** Remove 197746_3 as a separate issue on rent-deposit directions after an ex parte decree is set aside. The other five can stay together, or be split into 'before-filing revocation (not maintainable)' (404039_1, 404039_2) and 'after-filing or restored permission (maintainable)' (404039_3, 80590_1, 1472953_1).

## 134.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a later-enacted law or amendment restricting, invalidating or deeming the effect of transfers apply to a transfer completed before that law took effect, where the law is not expressly retrospective?

**Rule:** IF `transfer_proceeding_challenging_validity_or_effect_of_transfer and transfer_completed_before_later_law_took_effect and later_law_not_expressly_retrospective` THEN `later_law_does_not_apply_to_prior_transfer`

**Definition:** A statute or amendment that restricts, invalidates or deems the effect of transfers operates prospectively unless it says otherwise. It does not reach a transfer completed before it came into force, and that transfer is judged under the law then in force.

- `transfer_proceeding_challenging_validity_or_effect_of_transfer`: The proceeding questions the validity, legal effect or tax or ceiling treatment of a transfer, gift or surrender of property under a statutory restriction, ceiling or duty provision.
- `transfer_completed_before_later_law_took_effect`: The transfer was made and completed before the commencement of the later law, amendment or trigger period relied on to attack it or alter its treatment.
- `later_law_not_expressly_retrospective`: The later law, amendment or provision does not operate retrospectively by express words or necessary implication, and its operative period or reference excludes the earlier transfer.
- `later_law_does_not_apply_to_prior_transfer`: The later law or amendment does not govern, invalidate or alter the treatment of the earlier transfer, which is judged under the law in force when it was made.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In all five covered members the later provision was held not to apply to the earlier transfer, which survived. The sixth member (outlier) read down a recovery law to protect perfected titles.

**Recurring facts:** The transfer, gift or surrender took place before the commencement of the later statute or amendment.; The later provision either was not retrospective or named a specific earlier law or a later trigger period.; The later law was invoked to cancel, void or re-tax the earlier transfer.

**Provisions:** Section 50-B, Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, and Section 18, A.P. General Clauses Act; Sections 3(2) and 5, Rajasthan Urban Property (Restrictions of Transfers) Act, 1973, and its 1978 repeal; Section 5, Rajasthan Urban Property Ceiling Act, 1972; Section 10 proviso, Estate Duty Act, 1953, as amended by the Finance Act, 1965; Sections 6 and 40, Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973; Section 46, Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908; Sections 4 and 5 of a land-grant transfer recovery law (outlier)

**Exceptions/limits:** The rule does not apply where the later law is expressly or by necessary implication retrospective.; The earlier transfer must still comply with the law in force when it was made. One member noted that no breach of any other provision then in force had been shown.; Where the earlier regime itself restricts the transfer, for example by a restriction still in force and unperfected title, the transfer may still be affected under that earlier regime.; Some members add that the transfer must be bona fide, or that a statutory reference to a specific earlier law cannot be read as a later one.

**Split suggestion:** Keep the five prospectivity members together. Treat 1545120_2's cousin 1545120_5 (reading down a recovery law to protect perfected titles and non-breaching transfers) as a separate group on the scope and constitutional reading-down of transfer-recovery statutes.

## 128.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a joint Hindu family member's unilateral declaration of an intention to separate sever joint status only where the intention is clear and unequivocal and has been communicated or made known to the affected co-sharers?

**Rule:** IF `joint_hindu_family_severance_claim and unilateral_declaration_of_intention_to_separate and declaration_clear_and_unequivocal and intention_communicated_or_made_known_to_affected_members` THEN `joint_family_status_severed`

**Definition:** A member of a joint Hindu family may sever joint status unilaterally by a definite, unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate. The declaration takes effect only if it is brought to the knowledge of the affected co-sharers. An uncommunicated, conditional or equivocal declaration, including one in a trust deed or will, does not sever status.

- `joint_hindu_family_severance_claim`: A party asserts that a member's status in a joint Hindu family (Mitakshara coparcenary) was severed or that a separation or partition occurred.
- `unilateral_declaration_of_intention_to_separate`: A member, acting on his own, expressed in a document (trust deed, will, notice, deed of allotment) or by conduct an intention to hold his share separately.
- `declaration_clear_and_unequivocal`: The declaration is definite and unambiguous, is not merely conditional or contingent, and does not itself treat the property as remaining joint.
- `intention_communicated_or_made_known_to_affected_members`: The intention reached the knowledge of the co-sharers affected, by a process appropriate to the circumstances. This may be proved by actual notice, by knowledge of the contents, or by inference from the document, surrounding circumstances and subsequent conduct. Formal dispatch or receipt is not essential.
- `joint_family_status_severed`: The member's status in the joint family stands severed, whether or not the property has been divided by metes and bounds.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** Severance was held not to have occurred in 4 of 6 members (two trust-deed declarations never communicated, a will whose contents were not shown to have reached the affected member before the testator's death, and a will that was not unequivocal). Severance was held to have occurred in 2 of 6 members (an intercepted notice whose contents were known to the family, and a deed of allotment with exclusive enjoyment and subsequent conduct).

**Recurring facts:** A member of a Mitakshara joint family relied on a document (trust deed, will, notice or deed of allotment) as a declaration of an intention to separate.; The dispute was whether the intention was clear and unequivocal and whether it was communicated to or known by the affected co-sharers.; In several members the declaration was conditional or ambiguous, or was not shown to have reached the affected co-sharer.

**Provisions:** Mitakshara Hindu law of partition and severance of status; Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj; A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma; Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna; Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain; Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan

**Exceptions/limits:** An uncommunicated declaration is only an unexpressed intention and has no effect. Where the declarant dies before the affected member learns of it, no severance occurs.; A declaration that is conditional, or a will that treats the property as joint, directs it to remain joint, or denies that the property is ancestral, does not unequivocally express an intention to separate.; Communication need not take the form of formal dispatch or receipt. Knowledge of the contents is enough, and it may be inferred from the document, surrounding circumstances and subsequent conduct.; Once severance has occurred it cannot be undone by mere withdrawal of the communication, absent reunion.; Mere presence of an affected member's guardian in the house does not establish knowledge of the contents of the declaration.

## 36.3 (6 issues)

**Question:** Once a compensation determination, payment or related direction in land-acquisition matters has become final or been satisfied at an earlier stage, can it be reopened, recalled or reappropriated in later proceedings (reference, appeal, execution or fresh acquisition proceedings)?

**Rule:** IF `land_compensation_matter_in_later_proceeding and earlier_compensation_determination_or_payment_final_or_satisfied and later_proceeding_seeks_to_reopen_or_reallocate_that_earlier_matter and not (earlier_matter_void_for_want_of_jurisdiction or court_expressly_directs_otherwise)` THEN `earlier_final_or_satisfied_compensation_matter_not_reopened`

**Definition:** Compensation determinations, directions and payments in land acquisition that have become final or been satisfied at an earlier stage bind the parties and cannot be reopened, reappropriated or paid again in later reference, appellate, execution or acquisition proceedings. Only later enhancements or components, or jurisdictionally void orders, can be addressed afresh.

- `land_compensation_matter_in_later_proceeding`: The dispute arises in a later stage or proceeding (reference, appeal, execution, fresh determination or later acquisition proceeding) concerning compensation for acquired land.
- `earlier_compensation_determination_or_payment_final_or_satisfied`: An earlier award, valuation, court direction or payment or deposit of compensation has attained finality, for example through dismissal of a challenge, non-challenge or acting upon it, or has been satisfied or paid.
- `later_proceeding_seeks_to_reopen_or_reallocate_that_earlier_matter`: A party seeks to re-agitate, recompute, reappropriate or obtain repeat payment on the earlier final or satisfied matter, as distinct from dealing with a fresh enhancement or component.
- `earlier_matter_void_for_want_of_jurisdiction`: The earlier determination or award is a jurisdictional nullity (not merely erroneous), or the later enhancement or benefit was granted without jurisdiction, so that it can be challenged.
- `court_expressly_directs_otherwise`: The court expressly directs a different treatment, such as fresh determination of compensation.
- `earlier_final_or_satisfied_compensation_matter_not_reopened`: The earlier final or satisfied compensation matter stands and cannot be reopened, reappropriated or paid again in the later proceeding.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** About five of six members hold that the earlier final or satisfied matter cannot be reopened (finality, res judicata, no repeat compensation, no reappropriation). The sixth protects already-paid enhanced compensation from refund on fresh determination.

**Recurring facts:** An earlier award, valuation, direction or payment had become final or was satisfied.; A later stage (reference, appeal, execution or fresh acquisition proceeding) was invoked to reopen or reallocate it.; The party seeking to reopen had not challenged the earlier decision or had its challenge dismissed.

**Provisions:** Land Acquisition Act 1894 ss. 18, 23, 26, 28, 34, 53, 54; CPC s. 11 (res judicata), s. 47, Order XXI Rule 1; Article 226 of the Constitution; Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act 1972 s. 11

**Exceptions/limits:** A jurisdictional nullity, or a benefit or enhancement awarded without jurisdiction, may be challenged in execution (s.47 CPC) or set aside; mere error in exercising jurisdiction cannot be corrected in execution.; An unlawful later enhancement may be set aside even though the original award stays final.; Where the court sets aside decisions and orders fresh determination, it may expressly protect recipients from refund of enhanced amounts already paid; this is a direction protecting payments rather than reopening them.; Each later enhancement is dealt with at its own stage, with interest on the enhanced amount under the statutory scheme.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally separate 15173_6 (no refund of enhanced compensation on fresh determination) from the finality and non-reopening members. Keep ceiling-law double compensation (25681951_2) as a sub-group if a narrower rule is needed.

## 129.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Where a construction contract describes time as essential but also provides for extensions of time and/or delay compensation, is the completion period of the essence, and if not, is an employer's rescission for delay without first fixing a further reasonable period wrongful, so that it cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit?

**Rule:** IF `construction_contract_dispute and (contract_allows_extension or contract_provides_delay_compensation) and employer_rescinded_for_delay and employer_fixed_no_further_completion_period` THEN `rescission_wrongful_and_security_forfeiture_unavailable`

**Definition:** Even if a contract expressly says time is essential, extension and delay-compensation provisions can show that the completion period was not of the essence (or that the time was waived). An employer who rescinds for delay without first fixing a further reasonable period and making time essential for it acts wrongfully, and cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit, which must be refunded along with any established dues.

- `construction_contract_dispute`: The dispute arises out of a construction contract between an employer and a contractor.
- `contract_allows_extension`: The contract empowers the employer or its engineer to extend the completion period on reasonable grounds.
- `contract_provides_delay_compensation`: The contract provides for compensation for each day the work remains unfinished after the stipulated completion date.
- `employer_rescinded_for_delay`: The employer rescinded the contract on the ground that the contractor did not complete the work within the stipulated period.
- `employer_fixed_no_further_completion_period`: The employer did not give notice fixing a further reasonable period for completion and making time essential for that period before rescinding.
- `rescission_wrongful_and_security_forfeiture_unavailable`: The rescission is a wrongful breach by the employer, and the employer cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit on the basis of the contractor's alleged breach, so the deposit must be refunded.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All six members favour the contractor: in two, time is held not of the essence; in two, rescission is held wrongful and illegal; in two, forfeiture of the security deposit is disallowed and refund ordered (with unpaid balance and nominal damages in one). The cluster contains two duplicated sets of three issues.

**Recurring facts:** The contract described time as essential but allowed the engineer to extend the period and provided for compensation for delay.; The contractor was permitted to continue work after the stipulated period expired and sought extensions before it expired.; The employer rescinded without fixing a further period and making time essential.; The employer forfeited the contractor's security deposit on rescission.

**Provisions:** Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 4, para. 1179; Lamprell v. Billericay Union; Webb v. Hughes; Charles Rickards Ltd. v. Oppenheim; Clauses 2 and 6 of the contract (extension and delay compensation); No statutory provision cited

**Exceptions/limits:** Whether time is of the essence depends on the parties' intention from the contract as a whole; the rule applies only where the other terms displace the express time-essential stipulation or the stipulated time has been waived.; If time remained of the essence and was not waived or displaced, the requirement to fix a further period would not arise.; If the employer validly fixes a further reasonable period, makes time essential for it, and the contractor fails to complete within it, rescission may be justified.; Recovery of unpaid work and damages depends on the amounts being established, as found by the trial court in one member; nominal damages were restored there.

## 132.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Should a court decline to disturb a long-standing, settled judicial or administrative interpretation of a statute or legal rule when people have arranged their affairs and transactions in reliance on it?

**Rule:** IF `settled_interpretation_long_standing and reliance_on_interpretation_in_transactions_or_affairs and not interpretation_clearly_erroneous_or_compelling_reason_to_depart` THEN `settled_interpretation_should_be_followed_and_not_disturbed`

**Definition:** Where a statutory provision or rule has been uniformly interpreted over a long period and transactions or property titles rest on it, a court will ordinarily follow and not disturb that interpretation (stare decisis or deference to settled construction), unless it is clearly erroneous or a compelling or exceptional reason requires departure. Any anomalies are left to the legislature.

- `settled_interpretation_long_standing`: A statutory provision or legal rule has been consistently interpreted in the same way, by courts or by long-standing official practice, over a considerable period.
- `reliance_on_interpretation_in_transactions_or_affairs`: People have entered into transactions, property dealings or titles, or arranged their affairs, in reliance on the established interpretation, or unsettling it would plausibly upset such reliance.
- `interpretation_clearly_erroneous_or_compelling_reason_to_depart`: The established interpretation is patently or clearly erroneous (for example, contrary to clear statutory language), or there is an exceptional or compelling public-interest reason to depart from it.
- `settled_interpretation_should_be_followed_and_not_disturbed`: The court should adhere to and apply the established interpretation rather than adopt a different one, leaving any needed correction to the legislature.

**Coherence:** high · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 6 members leave the established interpretation or rule undisturbed and apply it, citing stare decisis, reliance and the need for certainty.

**Recurring facts:** An established interpretation had stood for a long period (decades in some cases).; Property transactions, titles or arrangements were made in reliance on that interpretation.; The challenge asked the court to adopt a different reading of a statute or rule.; Often the legislature amended related provisions without changing the relevant rule.; Several members involve local or State statutes (tenancy, building tax, money-lending, Hindu law alienations).

**Provisions:** Local building-tax statute (High Court interpretation); Municipal tax provision on tenant-built structures; Money-lending registration requirement; Bihar Tenancy Act and section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act; Local tenancy statute provisions on occupancy holdings; Hindu law rule on alienee's knowledge (Suraj Bunsi Koer)

**Exceptions/limits:** Does not apply where the interpretation is patently erroneous or contrary to clear statutory language and no titles or transactions have been founded on it.; Departure is permitted where public interest compels it.; Practice or usage does not bind a court to perpetuate a mistaken interpretation; long-standing practice is mainly an aid where the statute is obscure.; Deference to a High Court's reading of a local statute is ordinary, not absolute, and may serve only as an additional reason supporting the result.; Legislative inaction or amendment of other provisions without change to the relevant one is treated as supporting caution, but is not independently decisive.

## 26.5 (6 issues)

**Question:** Will the Supreme Court, on appeal, interfere with or accept a procedural-timeliness or alternative-remedy objection (delay, laches, or an available statutory remedy) where the court or authority below exercised its discretion to entertain the proceeding and the objection was not pressed or the delay was explained?

**Rule:** IF `appeal_before_supreme_court and procedural_objection_based_on_delay_or_alternative_remedy and (forum_below_exercised_discretion_to_entertain_or_accepted_explanation or objection_not_raised_or_pressed_earlier or no_statutory_limitation_period_applies) and not delay_alone_shown_to_vitiate_the_discretion` THEN `procedural_objection_not_accepted_and_discretionary_decision_not_disturbed`

**Definition:** Delay and the availability of an alternative remedy are matters of discretion for the forum below. The Supreme Court will not accept such an objection, or disturb the decision to entertain the proceeding, where the objection was not raised or pressed, the delay was explained and accepted, or no limitation period applies. Delay alone is not enough to set the decision aside.

- `appeal_before_supreme_court`: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal or special leave proceeding challenging the decision or the conduct of the proceeding below.
- `procedural_objection_based_on_delay_or_alternative_remedy`: A party objects that the proceeding should have been rejected because of delay in approaching the forum or because an alternative statutory remedy (such as an appeal) was available.
- `forum_below_exercised_discretion_to_entertain_or_accepted_explanation`: The High Court, revisional authority or lower court decided to entertain the delayed proceeding or accepted the explanation for the delay.
- `objection_not_raised_or_pressed_earlier`: The objector did not raise the objection in the appeal or did not seriously press it before the High Court.
- `no_statutory_limitation_period_applies`: The governing statute prescribes no limitation period for the proceeding, so timeliness is a matter of reasonableness left to the authority's discretion.
- `delay_alone_shown_to_vitiate_the_discretion`: Delay is the only ground, or is shown to be of such a kind that it by itself requires the discretionary decision to be set aside.
- `procedural_objection_not_accepted_and_discretionary_decision_not_disturbed`: The Supreme Court rejects or declines to entertain the delay or alternative-remedy objection and leaves the discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding undisturbed.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 5/6 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** In 5 of 6 members the Supreme Court rejected the delay or alternative-remedy objection or declined to disturb the discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding. In 1 member it refused to condone the petitioner's own delay.

**Recurring facts:** A proceeding was brought or entertained after substantial delay or despite an available alternative remedy.; The forum below (High Court or revisional authority) chose to entertain the proceeding or accepted the explanation for delay.; The objecting party did not raise or press the objection earlier, or the statute prescribed no limitation period.

**Provisions:** Article 226 of the Constitution (writ jurisdiction); Article 136 of the Constitution (special leave jurisdiction); Section 27, Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (revision at any time); Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874 (no limitation period for revision)

**Exceptions/limits:** Where the Supreme Court itself is asked to condone delay in approaching it, it may refuse condonation if it finds no merit in the explanation (209256_1).; Delay, particularly where third-party interests have intervened, remains relevant to how the discretion is exercised, and the alternative-remedy objection is noted as relevant even if not entertained.; Where no statutory period applies, the authority should normally act only within a reasonable time, and it is for that authority to judge what is reasonable.; The rule concerns non-interference with discretion. It does not hold that delay can never justify dismissal.

**Split suggestion:** Keep the five deference or non-entertainment members together. Treat 209256_1 (condonation of delay in filing a special leave petition) separately, together with other condonation-of-delay cases. Optionally separate the alternative-remedy member (164655261_2) from the delay members.

## 142.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Can a person be held in contempt (or penalised) for non-compliance where the order or legal obligation was unclear, undecided, or never undertaken, and the person acted on a bona fide understanding, so that wilful disobedience is not established?

**Rule:** IF `(contempt_or_penal_proceeding and alleged_breach_alleged) and (wilful_disobedience_not_established_beyond_reasonable_doubt) and (order_or_obligation_did_not_clearly_impose_the_duty_alleged_to_be_breached or bona_fide_reasonable_understanding_by_alleged_defaulter)` THEN `contempt_or_penalty_not_sustained_and_remedy_left_to_other_proceedings`

**Definition:** Contempt, a quasi-criminal remedy, or a penalty requires wilful, deliberate non-compliance with a clear order or obligation. Where the order was ambiguous or undecided on the point, no undertaking was actually given, or the person acted on a bona fide reasonable understanding of the order or an uncertain law, the breach is not sustained and the underlying dispute is left to execution or other remedies.

- `contempt_or_penal_proceeding`: The proceeding seeks to punish the person, by contempt or by a penalty, for non-compliance with an order or legal obligation.
- `alleged_breach_alleged`: The applicant or authority alleges failure to comply with a court order, undertaking, or statutory obligation.
- `wilful_disobedience_not_established_beyond_reasonable_doubt`: The record does not prove deliberate or wilful disobedience to the standard required for contempt, or deliberate or dishonest default in the penalty context.
- `order_or_obligation_did_not_clearly_impose_the_duty_alleged_to_be_breached`: The order did not decide the liability, did not contain the direction alleged, was a consent order without a recorded undertaking, or no undertaking was given, or the legal position was uncertain.
- `bona_fide_reasonable_understanding_by_alleged_defaulter`: The alleged defaulter acted on a genuine and reasonable understanding of the order or law, where competing interpretations were possible or the legal position was uncertain.
- `contempt_or_penalty_not_sustained_and_remedy_left_to_other_proceedings`: Contempt action or penalty is not warranted or is set aside, and any underlying claim may be pursued through execution or other lawful proceedings.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 6/6 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 6 members found that the breach or penalty was not sustained: 5 contempt matters were dismissed or the conviction set aside, with disputed claims left to execution or other proceedings, and 1 tax penalty was set aside.

**Recurring facts:** The alleged breach concerned an order that was ambiguous, did not decide the point, or was a consent order.; No undertaking was recorded in the court.; The alleged contemner acted on a bona fide interpretation of the order.; An alternative remedy such as execution was available.; In the tax case, the law was uncertain and the taxpayer bona fide excluded the disputed amounts.

**Provisions:** Article 129 of the Constitution; Sections 2(b), 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; Code of Civil Procedure execution provisions (consent orders)

**Exceptions/limits:** Does not apply where the order is clear and the disobedience is wilful and proved beyond reasonable doubt.; Does not apply where an undertaking was in fact expressly given to the court, in writing or orally and recorded; its wilful breach can be contempt.; The finding is on wilfulness only and does not decide the underlying liability, which remains open in execution or other proceedings.; The tax-penalty member applies the bona fide belief principle outside contempt, and only where the legal position was genuinely uncertain.

**Split suggestion:** If a tighter cluster is wanted: (a) contempt where the order is ambiguous or the interpretation bona fide (18545704_2, 18545704_3, 403270_2); (b) contempt where no undertaking was given (458739_1, 615500_2); (c) tax penalty for bona fide non-inclusion under uncertain law (996616_3).

## 140.0 (6 issues)

**Question:** Does a merger covenant recognizing a former ruler's property as private property, or guaranteeing its enjoyment, prevent the State from acquiring that property under a law that treats it as private property, and can a court adjudicate a challenge based on the covenant?
