- `late_deposit_within_application_period_is_sufficient_and_sale_may_be_set_aside`: A deposit made after 30 days but within the 60-day application period does not bar the application; the sale is liable to be set aside, or the court has discretion to set it aside, on the merits.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 2/3 shown · outliers 1

**Typical outcome:** Two of the three members (1689577_1, 672592_1) hold that a deposit within the 60-day application period suffices; one of these makes the grant discretionary. One member (1544426_1) holds that the deposit must be made within 30 days, and it allowed the auction-purchaser's appeal.

**Recurring facts:** Immovable property was sold in execution of a decree.; An application to set aside the sale was made with a deposit under Order XXI Rule 89.; The deposit was made after 30 days but within 60 days of the sale, and the auction-purchaser objected that it was late.; The Article 127 period was extended from 30 to 60 days by the 1976 amendment.

**Provisions:** Order XXI Rules 89, 90 and 92(2), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; Article 127, Limitation Act, 1963 (60 days, as amended by Act 104 of 1976)

**Exceptions/limits:** Under the contrary line (1544426_1), the deposit is a condition precedent to the application and must be made within 30 days of the sale under Rule 92(2). The 60-day period under Article 127 governs only the application, so a deposit after 30 days is out of time.; Where the deposit or application falls outside the 60-day Article 127 period, even the more lenient view gives no relief.; Under 672592_1, a deposit made after the first 30 days but within 60 days leaves the court with discretion whether to allow the application. The set-aside is not automatic, whereas a deposit within 30 days removes that discretion.; Courts must apply clear statutory text without adding words. The members differ on whether Rule 92(2) is clear enough to bar a later deposit.

**Split suggestion:** The members share one legal question but give conflicting answers. Treat 1689577_1 and 672592_1 (deposit allowed within 60 days, the latter with discretion) as one line and 1544426_1 (strict 30-day deposit) as the opposing line. 672592_1 could be separated further as the discretion variant.

## 368.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When a deed of transfer states an absolute transfer and contains no term making the transfer conditional, temporary or security-based, is it construed as an outright, unconditional transfer of title, so that a party asserting a condition or a nominal character fails?

**Rule:** IF `transfer_deed_in_dispute and deed_terms_express_absolute_or_unconditional_transfer and no_condition_or_return_term_in_deed and not surrounding_circumstances_show_contrary_intention` THEN `deed_operates_as_outright_unconditional_transfer`

**Definition:** A deed that on its terms transfers property absolutely, and contains no condition, return clause or security character, is construed according to its plain terms as an outright transfer. The party asserting a condition, nominal character or provisional transfer must show it from the deed or from surrounding circumstances, and cannot read a condition into the deed contrary to its terms.

- `transfer_deed_in_dispute`: The dispute concerns the legal effect or character of a deed transferring immovable property (sale, exchange or allocation).
- `deed_terms_express_absolute_or_unconditional_transfer`: On its plain terms the deed transfers the property absolutely, for consideration or in exchange for other rights, and relinquishes the transferor's remaining interest or claims.
- `no_condition_or_return_term_in_deed`: The deed contains no term making the transfer conditional on payment or further performance, no term making it provisional or temporary, and no term for return of the property. A separate same-day agreement to reconvey does not by itself supply such a term.
- `surrounding_circumstances_show_contrary_intention`: Evidence outside the deed, such as conduct, possession or contemporaneous documents, establishes that the parties intended the transfer to be conditional, provisional or only a security.
- `deed_operates_as_outright_unconditional_transfer`: The deed is held to pass title or ownership outright and unconditionally. A claim that it was conditional, nominal, provisional or security only is rejected.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold the deed to be an outright, unconditional transfer and reject the challenge, based on the deed's plain terms.

**Recurring facts:** A written deed with clear terms of absolute transfer or allocation.; The party challenging the deed alleges it was conditional, nominal, provisional or security only.; The deed has no express condition or return term.; Possession was delivered to or held by the transferee.; Collateral circumstances such as a mortgage, a retained receipt or a reconveyance agreement did not displace the deed's terms.

**Provisions:** Transfer of Property Act 1882, Sections 8, 54 and 58(c); Evidence Act, Section 92

**Exceptions/limits:** If the deed expressly makes passage of title conditional on payment or performance, the condition governs (the Panchoo Sahu illustration in the sale-deed member).; If the deed is ambiguous, surrounding circumstances may be used to find a different intention, subject to Section 92 of the Evidence Act.; Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, a sale and an agreement to reconvey embodied in the same document may amount to a mortgage by conditional sale. Separate documents executed the same day do not.; Under Sections 8 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, title passes on a registered sale unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied.

## 331.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When can a family co-sharer invoke the statutory right under Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 (read with Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882) to buy an outsider transferee's share in an undivided family dwelling house, and when is that right not available because the transferee has not sought partition or the decree has been fully executed?

**Rule:** IF `undivided_family_dwelling_house and share_transferred_to_outsider and family_shareholder_seeks_to_purchase and outsider_transferee_seeks_partition_or_separate_possession and not partition_decree_fully_executed` THEN `statutory_preemption_right_available`

**Definition:** A family shareholder may buy an outsider transferee's share in an undivided family dwelling house under Section 4 of the Partition Act once the transferee sues for partition, which includes seeking execution of a partition decree. The right is not available if the transferee has not sought partition and separate possession (the application is premature), nor after the decree has been fully executed and possession delivered.

- `undivided_family_dwelling_house`: The property is a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family and still held in common.
- `share_transferred_to_outsider`: A share in the dwelling house has been transferred to a person who is not a member of the family.
- `family_shareholder_seeks_to_purchase`: A family shareholder applies to buy the outsider transferee's share.
- `outsider_transferee_seeks_partition_or_separate_possession`: The outsider transferee sues for partition, including by pursuing execution of a partition decree, to obtain separation and possession of the share. Merely asserting a share does not satisfy this.
- `partition_decree_fully_executed`: The partition decree has been fully executed and satisfied by division by metes and bounds and delivery of possession to the respective shareholders.
- `statutory_preemption_right_available`: The family shareholder's application to purchase the outsider's share under Section 4 of the Partition Act is maintainable.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** The three members delimit the temporal scope of the right. One (155465_1) holds the application maintainable while execution is incomplete. One (155465_2) holds the remedy unavailable after full execution. One (240013_2) holds the application premature because the transferee has not sought partition.

**Recurring facts:** A dwelling house belonging to an undivided family; A share transferred to a non-member (stranger) transferee; A family co-sharer seeking to buy the transferee's share; The stage of the partition proceedings (not yet sought, pending execution, or fully executed) determines the outcome

**Provisions:** Section 4, Partition Act, 1893; Section 44, Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Section 38 and Order 21 Rule 16, Order 22 Rules 10 and 12, Explanation VII to Section 11, CPC; Explanation to Section 52, Transfer of Property Act (as relied on in 155465_1); Ghantesher Ghosh v. Madan Mohan Ghosh

**Exceptions/limits:** If the transferee only asserts a share and does not seek partition or separation and possession, the application is premature and fails. It may be renewed if the transferee later seeks partition.; Once the decree is fully executed by division by metes and bounds and delivery of possession, the dwelling house no longer belongs to an undivided family as to the separated portion, and the remedy ends.; The right depends on the property being a dwelling house of an undivided family and the transferee being a stranger to the family.

## 332.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When is an owner whose land is partly acquired entitled to compensation for severance or for injurious effect on the remaining property?

**Rule:** IF `land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and part_of_property_acquired and remainder_left_with_owner and claimant_seeks_compensation_for_remainder_damage and acquisition_caused_damage_to_remainder` THEN `severance_or_injurious_effect_compensation_allowed`

**Definition:** Where part of a property is acquired, the owner may claim, in a compensation reference, additional compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder. The claim succeeds if the acquisition caused damage to the remainder, such as diminished value. It fails if the damage is unproved or pre-existed the acquisition.

- `land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding`: The matter is a compulsory acquisition compensation proceeding, including a reference to the court for determining compensation.
- `part_of_property_acquired`: Only part of the owner's land or property was acquired.
- `remainder_left_with_owner`: A portion of the property remains with the owner after acquisition.
- `claimant_seeks_compensation_for_remainder_damage`: The claimant claims compensation for severance or for the acquisition injuriously affecting the remaining property or earnings.
- `acquisition_caused_damage_to_remainder`: The claimant has established, by evidence or reasonable inference, that the acquisition itself diminished the value or usefulness of the remaining property. Pre-existing conditions or unproved expenditure do not satisfy this.
- `severance_or_injurious_effect_compensation_allowed`: The claimant is entitled to compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder, and the claim may be considered in the compensation reference.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** Two of the three members allow or permit consideration of compensation for damage to the remainder (1690721_3, 444729_3). One denies it for failure of proof (1559215_4).

**Recurring facts:** Only part of the claimant's property was acquired and a remainder was left with the owner.; The claimant sought additional compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder.; The existence of access or an entrance to the remainder featured in the reasoning.

**Provisions:** Section 23(1), including its third and fourth clauses (severance and injurious affection); Section 18 (reference to court); Section 49 (acquisition of the whole building, distinguished)

**Exceptions/limits:** Compensation is denied where the claimed expenditure on protective works is not substantiated by accounts or other material.; Compensation is denied where the alleged impairment, such as water stagnation, existed before the acquisition or is otherwise unsubstantiated.; Retention of an entrance or access to the remainder does not by itself defeat a severance claim, but continued usability of access may show that no damage was caused.; A claim for additional compensation for injury to remaining property is distinct from a request to acquire the whole building under the separate provision.

## 354.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When compensating for acquired land that bears fruit-bearing trees, may the claimant receive a separate award for the trees' potential or income value on top of the land's market value, or does that double-count the same value?

**Rule:** IF `land_acquisition_compensation_case and land_bears_fruit_trees and land_value_assessed_to_include_land_potential_or_tree_yield and separate_award_claimed_or_made_for_tree_value_beyond_salvage` THEN `separate_tree_value_beyond_salvage_not_allowed`

**Definition:** Where land bearing fruit trees is valued on its potential or by capitalizing the trees' yield, a separate award for the trees' potential or income value duplicates the land value and is not allowed. At most the trees may be valued as timber or firewood, net of salvage expenses.

- `land_acquisition_compensation_case`: The dispute concerns determining compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
- `land_bears_fruit_trees`: The acquired land contains fruit-bearing trees.
- `land_value_assessed_to_include_land_potential_or_tree_yield`: The land's market value has been (or is to be) fixed on its potential and advantages, or by capitalizing the income or yield from its fruit trees, or the claimant has confined the claim to the land's market value.
- `separate_award_claimed_or_made_for_tree_value_beyond_salvage`: A further, separate amount is claimed or was awarded for the trees' potential value or capitalized income, beyond their timber, firewood or salvage value.
- `separate_tree_value_beyond_salvage_not_allowed`: No separate compensation for the trees' potential or capitalized income value may be awarded; at most the trees may be valued as timber or firewood after deducting salvage expenses.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members refuse a separate award for the trees' potential or income value. One rests on abandonment by the claimant and two on avoiding double counting, with the trees valued only as timber or firewood or at salvage.

**Recurring facts:** Acquired land bore fruit-bearing trees such as coconut, arecanut and pepper.; A separate amount for the trees was claimed or awarded in addition to the land value.; Land value was fixed on potential or on yield.

**Provisions:** Land Acquisition Act 1894, section 3(a) (land includes benefits arising from it); State of Kerala v. P.P. Hassan Koya; Special Land Acquisition Officer v. P. Veerabhadarappa; Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi

**Exceptions/limits:** One of the two valuation methods must be chosen: the land valued with its potential and advantages with trees only at salvage value, or the land valued by capitalizing reliable annual net income from the trees. They cannot be combined.; The first member rests on the claimant's concession (abandonment) when confining the claim to land value. It states no broader rule on tree valuation.; Capitalizing tree income requires reliable evidence of actual or immediately prospective net annual income.

## 398.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a retired armed-forces member, or a relation claiming through such a member, use a special eviction procedure or deemed-need presumption for service personnel when the statutory conditions tying the benefit to the member's service, or to letting before retirement, are not met?

**Rule:** IF `special_service_based_eviction_benefit_invoked and not statutory_service_linked_condition_satisfied` THEN `special_benefit_unavailable`

**Definition:** Special eviction procedures and deemed-need presumptions for armed-forces landlords or their dependants are confined to the cases the statute describes. Where the statutory condition is missing, for example the premises were not let before retirement or the member is retired and alive, the benefit cannot be claimed.

- `special_service_based_eviction_benefit_invoked`: The applicant seeks possession under a special eviction procedure, remedy or deemed-need presumption that a statute reserves for armed-forces or service personnel (or their dependants).
- `statutory_service_linked_condition_satisfied`: The applicant meets the specific condition the statute attaches to the benefit, such as the member dying in service or within the stated period after retirement, or the premises having been let by the member as landlord during service or before retirement.
- `special_benefit_unavailable`: The applicant cannot rely on the special procedure, remedy or deemed presumption, though any ordinary remedy or independently proved ground may remain.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 3 members the special benefit was denied for failure to meet the statutory condition. One case preserved other remedies and another upheld the decree on independent need.

**Recurring facts:** The claimant is a retired armed-forces member or a dependant of one.; The claimant seeks recovery of premises through a special service-based procedure, remedy or presumption.; The statutory condition linking the benefit to service or to pre-retirement letting is absent.

**Provisions:** West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, ss. 13(1)(ff) and 29B; Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, s. 13A1(a); U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, s. 21(1), Explanation (iii); Article 14 (read-down rationale in the Bombay case)

**Exceptions/limits:** The unavailability applies only to the special procedure or presumption. Other remedies, or an independently proved bona fide need, may still succeed, as in the U.P. case where the possession decree stood on independently established need.; The Bombay case expressly left open the position of a person who becomes landlord while still serving, by acquiring premises already tenanted.; The exact condition differs by statute, so the court must check the particular provision's wording.

## 448.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Does a transferee in possession who has performed or is willing to perform a contract acquire, under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, only a defensive right to resist the transferor, without ownership or title enforceable against others?

**Rule:** IF `section_53A_part_performance_claimed and transferee_in_possession_in_part_performance and transferee_performed_or_willing_to_perform and no_completed_conveyance` THEN `protection_is_limited_to_defending_possession_against_transferor_and_no_ownership_or_active_title_arises`

**Definition:** Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act gives a transferee who is in possession and has performed or is willing to perform only a defensive bar against the transferor and those claiming under the transferor. It does not confer ownership or active title, and it cannot be asserted against third parties or to override an overriding statutory regime.

- `section_53A_part_performance_claimed`: The transferee relies on the doctrine of part performance under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
- `transferee_in_possession_in_part_performance`: The transferee took or continued in possession of the property on the basis of the contract, in part performance of it.
- `transferee_performed_or_willing_to_perform`: The transferee has performed, or is ready and willing to perform, their obligations under the contract.
- `no_completed_conveyance`: No valid completed transfer or conveyance of title has been executed in the transferee's favour.
- `protection_is_limited_to_defending_possession_against_transferor_and_no_ownership_or_active_title_arises`: The transferee has only a shield against the transferor, or persons claiming under the transferor, to resist disturbance of possession. The transferee gets no ownership or active title and no right enforceable against third parties.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold that section 53A gives only a shield or defensive right to protect possession against the transferor, and no ownership or active title. One member adds that it cannot be asserted against third parties, and another that it does not override special rehabilitation law.

**Recurring facts:** The transferee was in possession under a contract or agreement to transfer or lease that was not completed by a valid conveyance.; The transferee relied on part performance to resist the transferor or a restriction on completing the transfer.; The transferee had performed or was willing to perform the contract.

**Provisions:** Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act, 1882

**Exceptions/limits:** The protection applies only if the statutory conditions for part performance are met (contract, possession, performance or willingness to perform).; The protection operates against the transferor or persons claiming under the transferor, not against third parties.; Where a special statute, such as a rehabilitation law, conflicts with the general property-transfer law, the special law prevails over a part-performance claim.

## 334.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a party's consent, acquiescence, admission, waiver or failure to object confer jurisdiction on a court or tribunal that lacks it (inherent or subject-matter jurisdiction, or jurisdiction dependent on a mandatory statutory requirement), or validate its decision?

**Rule:** IF `forum_lacks_jurisdiction_or_authority_due_to_inherent_or_statutory_limit and party_consented_acquiesced_admitted_or_failed_to_object` THEN `party_conduct_does_not_confer_jurisdiction_or_validate_decision`

**Definition:** Where a court or tribunal lacks jurisdiction because of an inherent or subject-matter limit or a mandatory statutory requirement, a party's consent, acquiescence, admission, waiver or failure to object cannot supply that jurisdiction or validate what the forum did. Such an order is a nullity.

- `forum_lacks_jurisdiction_or_authority_due_to_inherent_or_statutory_limit`: The court or tribunal lacks jurisdiction or authority that goes to its inherent competence, to the subject matter, or to a mandatory statutory requirement (such as its composition or its permitted role), as opposed to a mere territorial or pecuniary irregularity.
- `party_consented_acquiesced_admitted_or_failed_to_object`: The party who later challenges the forum's jurisdiction earlier consented, acquiesced, admitted jurisdiction, waived the point, or failed to object at the proper time.
- `party_conduct_does_not_confer_jurisdiction_or_validate_decision`: The party's consent, acquiescence, admission, waiver or silence does not give the forum the missing jurisdiction, does not validate its order or findings, and does not bar the party from challenging them.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold that consent, acquiescence or failure to object does not cure the want of jurisdiction.

**Recurring facts:** A party had acquiesced, admitted jurisdiction or failed to object, and later challenged or relied on the forum's lack of jurisdiction.; The defect arose from a statutory or inherent limit on the forum's power: the appellate bench's role, the tribunal's composition, or the court's subject-matter competence.

**Provisions:** Sections 58, 59 and 60, Punjab Improvement Trust Act, 1922; Section 21, Code of Civil Procedure (contrasted for territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction); Ledgard v. Bull; Meenakshi Naidoo v. Subramaniya Sastri; Bahrein Petroleum v. Pappu; Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan; Setrucharlu v. Maharaja of Jeypore

**Exceptions/limits:** Applies to inherent or subject-matter jurisdiction and mandatory statutory requirements, not to mere territorial or pecuniary defects.; Objections to territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction must be raised at the earliest opportunity, and by or before settlement of issues where Section 21 CPC applies; failure to do so can bar them.; The members rest on the nature of the defect (inherent, subject-matter or mandatory statutory), so the rule does not cover procedural irregularities that are curable.

## 363.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Where a High Court appellate forum (a Division Bench in a Letters Patent or intra-court appeal, or a second appellate court) is dealing with a matter that turns on facts or on construction of documents, does it have the power to re-examine those questions and reach its own conclusion despite the findings of the court below?

**Rule:** IF `(appellate_forum_is_high_court_intra_court_or_letters_patent_appeal and decision_appealed_was_by_single_judge_exercising_appellate_jurisdiction and question_is_fact_or_mixed_fact_and_law_or_document_construction) or (proceeding_is_second_appeal and document_construction_is_question_of_law_going_to_root_of_dispute and issue_not_directly_determined_by_lower_courts)` THEN `appellate_forum_may_reexamine_the_question_and_decide_it_independently`

**Definition:** A bench hearing a Letters Patent or intra-court appeal from a single judge's decision in a first appeal has the same powers as the first appellate court, and so can reconsider facts, law and mixed questions including document construction. A second appellate court can likewise examine foundational document construction as a question of law and decide an undetermined issue under section 103 CPC.

- `appellate_forum_is_high_court_intra_court_or_letters_patent_appeal`: The appeal is heard by a Division Bench or later bench of the High Court as an intra-court appeal, including under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent.
- `decision_appealed_was_by_single_judge_exercising_appellate_jurisdiction`: The decision under appeal was given by a single judge deciding a first appeal from a trial court.
- `question_is_fact_or_mixed_fact_and_law_or_document_construction`: The point in dispute involves questions of fact, or a mixed question of law and fact such as construing documents in light of surrounding circumstances.
- `proceeding_is_second_appeal`: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure.
- `document_construction_is_question_of_law_going_to_root_of_dispute`: The construction of foundational documents is a question of law that goes to the root of the dispute.
- `issue_not_directly_determined_by_lower_courts`: The lower courts did not directly decide the issue, such as whether leave to compromise was obtained by fraud.
- `appellate_forum_may_reexamine_the_question_and_decide_it_independently`: The appellate forum has the power to reconsider the question and reach its own conclusion, and doing so is not an error.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members uphold the High Court appellate forum's power to re-examine the question (2 intra-court or Letters Patent appeals, 1 second appeal).

**Recurring facts:** Disputes over title, possession or religious and charitable endowments, with concurrent or earlier findings against the appellant; Outcome depends on construction of documents such as grants, trust deeds and agreements; High Court appellate bench disturbed or re-examined an earlier finding

**Provisions:** Clause 10 of the Letters Patent; Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure; Section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure; Asha Devi v. Dukhi Sao, AIR 1974 SC 2048

**Exceptions/limits:** The second-appeal route is limited to questions of law, including document construction that is a question of law going to the root of the dispute; it does not extend to general re-appreciation of evidence.; Under section 103 CPC, the second appellate court's power to decide an issue the lower courts did not determine rests on the issue turning on the document construction and on the lower courts having left it undetermined.; The wide Letters Patent power applies where the single judge acted as a first appellate court; it is not confined by section 100 CPC.; An intra-court appeal differs from an appeal against a subordinate court's order, in which the High Court acts as a court of error.

**Split suggestion:** If a narrower rule is required, split into (a) Letters Patent or intra-court appeal powers (1571903_1, 1855408_1) and (b) second appellate court powers under sections 100 and 103 CPC (477701_3).

## 336.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When a person (tenant or party in possession) has been wrongfully or unlawfully dispossessed within the period and manner the statute covers, is the person entitled to be restored to possession, or treated as in possession, under the statutory restoration mechanism?

**Rule:** IF `statutory_restoration_proceeding and dispossessed_within_statutory_scope_without_lawful_termination and statutory_conditions_for_restoration_met and not statutory_bar_to_restoration` THEN `dispossessed_party_entitled_to_restoration_or_deemed_possession`

**Definition:** Where a claimant has been dispossessed in a way the statute covers, without lawful termination of the right, and meets the statutory conditions with no statutory bar, the statutory mechanism restores possession or treats the claimant as in possession. Later events, such as trespass and ejectment, and the physical consequences of the restoration do not defeat the entitlement or recharacterise the proceeding.

- `statutory_restoration_proceeding`: The claim is brought under a statutory provision that provides for restoring possession to, or treating as in possession, a person who has been dispossessed.
- `dispossessed_within_statutory_scope_without_lawful_termination`: The claimant was dispossessed in a manner and within a period covered by the statute (for example, by surrender or sale that did not lawfully end the tenancy, or by forcible and wrongful dispossession within the prescribed period).
- `statutory_conditions_for_restoration_met`: The procedural or substantive requirements the statute lays down for restoration are satisfied (for example, entitlement certificate, deposit and application, or the proviso's conditions).
- `statutory_bar_to_restoration`: A statutory bar applies, such as a qualifying sale to a bona fide purchaser for consideration, or a lawful termination of the tenancy.
- `dispossessed_party_entitled_to_restoration_or_deemed_possession`: The dispossessed party is entitled to restoration of possession, or to be treated as in possession on the relevant date, and that relief is not displaced by a later event or a different statutory regime.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All three members favour the dispossessed party: two order restoration of possession to a tenant (15862952_4, 22645_3), and one holds that restoration under s. 145 only gives effect to deemed possession and is not a barred eviction (1656455_2).

**Recurring facts:** The claimant had been dispossessed through a transaction or act that did not lawfully end their right (alleged surrender, auction sale, forcible dispossession).; The dispossession fell within a statutory window or category.; The opposing party held possession and might have to give it up.

**Provisions:** Telangana Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, s. 38-E(1) explanation and s. 38-E(2); Section 13(B)(1) and its proviso (restoration after a rent-arrears execution sale); Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, s. 145(4) proviso and s. 145(6)(a); Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, ss. 4 and 8

**Exceptions/limits:** Restoration is unavailable where a statutory bar applies, such as a bona fide purchaser for consideration.; Restoration requires the statutory preconditions, such as deposit and application, dispossession within the prescribed period, or a certificate.; The section 145 CrPC member concerns deeming possession to prevent a breach of the peace; it does not decide title or amount to eviction.; The statute-specific provisions differ (tenancy statutes versus the CrPC), so the precise conditions depend on the governing provision.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally separate 1656455_2 (s. 145 CrPC deemed possession versus eviction under the vacant-lands statute) from the two tenancy restoration members (15862952_4 and 22645_3), which share a tighter rule on a tenant's entitlement to restoration.

## 337.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When is a deceased person's out-of-court statement against his or her own proprietary interest admissible under sections 21 and 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act, particularly as evidence against those claiming through the declarant?

**Rule:** IF `property_dispute and declarant_is_dead and statement_is_against_declarants_proprietary_interest and declarant_knew_statement_was_adverse_to_own_interest and statement_is_used_against_declarant_or_those_claiming_through_declarant` THEN `statement_is_admissible_as_evidence_against_proprietary_interest`

**Definition:** A statement by a deceased person that is against his or her own proprietary interest is admissible under sections 21 and 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act, provided the declarant knew it was adverse. It may be used against the declarant and those claiming through him or her, but not in the declarant's own favour.

- `property_dispute`: The proceeding is a civil dispute about title to, ownership of, or interest in property (including a dispute over whether a purchase was benami).
- `declarant_is_dead`: The person who made the statement is dead and cannot be examined.
- `statement_is_against_declarants_proprietary_interest`: When made, the statement went against the declarant's own proprietary (or pecuniary) interest, for example by disclaiming ownership or by placing the declarant in a position with no proprietary right.
- `declarant_knew_statement_was_adverse_to_own_interest`: The declarant knew, or knowledge can be inferred from the circumstances, that the statement was against his or her own interest.
- `statement_is_used_against_declarant_or_those_claiming_through_declarant`: The statement is relied on against the declarant, or against the declarant's legal representative or successor claiming through him or her, and not in the declarant's own favour.
- `statement_is_admissible_as_evidence_against_proprietary_interest`: The statement is admissible in evidence under sections 21 and 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All three members held the statement admissible as evidence against the declarant's proprietary interest, and against the declarant's representative where relevant.

**Recurring facts:** The declarant was dead when the statement was tendered.; The statement was against the declarant's own proprietary interest.; The party opposing the statement was the declarant's representative or claimed through the declarant.; Two members involve a deceased purchaser or contributor who said, after the purchase, that the house belonged to another person.; One member involves a widow's statement in an earlier suit that placed her in a position with no proprietary right.

**Provisions:** Indian Evidence Act 1872, section 21; Indian Evidence Act 1872, section 32(3); Shephard v. Cartwright, distinguished in two members; Srimati Savitri Debi v. Raman Bijoy, Tucker v. Oldbury Urban District Council and Ward v. H. S. Pitt, relied on in one member

**Exceptions/limits:** Admissibility rests on the declarant's knowledge that the statement was against his or her interest. This is a question of fact, usually inferred from the circumstances.; Later declarations are not admissible in the maker's own favour, following the rule discussed in Shephard v. Cartwright. They are admissible only against the maker or those claiming through the maker.; The statement must actually be against the declarant's proprietary or pecuniary interest when made.

## 388.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Does the presence of blood on an accused's clothing or footwear, without evidence linking it to the victim or excluding an innocent explanation such as later presence at the scene, prove or corroborate the accused's participation in the crime?

**Rule:** IF `criminal_case_against_accused and blood_found_on_accused_clothing_or_footwear and (blood_not_linked_to_deceased_or_crime or blood_consistent_with_innocent_explanation_such_as_post_crime_presence) and not independent_evidence_proves_participation` THEN `blood_evidence_does_not_prove_or_corroborate_participation`

**Definition:** Blood on an accused's clothing or footwear has no probative value toward participation in the crime if it is not linked to the deceased or if it is equally explained by innocent or post-crime presence at the scene. It cannot corroborate a witness or establish concert or common intention absent other independent evidence.

- `criminal_case_against_accused`: The case is a criminal prosecution or appeal from conviction in which the accused's participation in the offence is in issue.
- `blood_found_on_accused_clothing_or_footwear`: Blood stains or traces were detected on clothing or footwear taken from or worn by the accused.
- `blood_not_linked_to_deceased_or_crime`: The evidence does not identify the blood group or otherwise connect the blood to the deceased or the offence (e.g. only 'human blood' is reported).
- `blood_consistent_with_innocent_explanation_such_as_post_crime_presence`: The blood could have been acquired innocently, for example by the accused being taken to or present at the bloodstained scene after the crime, or from the accused's own blood.
- `independent_evidence_proves_participation`: Other reliable evidence independently establishes the accused's participation or prior concert in the crime.
- `blood_evidence_does_not_prove_or_corroborate_participation`: The blood evidence cannot be used to connect the accused to the crime, to corroborate a witness's allegation of participation, or to establish common intention.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 3 members the blood evidence was held insufficient to connect the accused to the crime or to corroborate participation or common intention.

**Recurring facts:** Blood was found on the accused's clothing or footwear.; The blood was not tied to the deceased by blood group or other evidence, or could be explained by post-crime presence at the scene.; There was no other sufficient independent evidence of participation or concert.

**Provisions:** Sections 3 and 14, Indian Evidence Act, 1872; Section 34, Indian Penal Code (common intention)

**Exceptions/limits:** The rule does not apply where independent evidence proves participation or prior concert.; The rule does not apply where the blood is positively linked to the deceased (e.g. by matching blood group) and no plausible innocent explanation exists.; In the footwear member the innocent explanation had to be plausible on the facts (the accused were taken to the bloodstained scene before seizure); a purely speculative explanation may not suffice.

## 405.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a party to a written sale deed or sale agreement lead oral or extrinsic evidence, or rely on other material, to contradict or vary the terms recorded in the document (such as the price or the nature of the transaction), or must the document be taken to record the transaction as written?

**Rule:** IF `written_document_between_parties_records_sale_terms and party_seeks_to_contradict_or_vary_recorded_terms_by_oral_or_extrinsic_evidence and not contrary_account_is_supported_by_persuasive_evidence_or_a_recognised_exception` THEN `recorded_written_terms_prevail_and_contrary_claim_is_rejected`

**Definition:** Where parties have reduced a sale to writing, a party cannot use oral statements, alleged side-agreements or other extrinsic material to contradict the recorded price or recharacterise the transaction. The document is read according to its recitals and terms, and a contrary account that rests on vague oral evidence or surmise is rejected.

- `written_document_between_parties_records_sale_terms`: The parties to the dispute are parties to a written sale deed or sale agreement that states the terms of the sale, such as the price, payments or the nature of the transaction.
- `party_seeks_to_contradict_or_vary_recorded_terms_by_oral_or_extrinsic_evidence`: A party relies on an oral account, an alleged oral agreement or other extrinsic material, such as a stamp valuation, to contradict, vary, add to or subtract from what the document records.
- `contrary_account_is_supported_by_persuasive_evidence_or_a_recognised_exception`: The contrary account is backed by persuasive evidence, or the case falls within a recognised exception to the bar on varying written terms, so that the written terms are not conclusive.
- `recorded_written_terms_prevail_and_contrary_claim_is_rejected`: The court treats the document as recording the transaction according to its terms and rejects the claim that the price or nature of the transaction was different.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 3 members the written terms prevail and the contrary claim is rejected: the agreements are held to be sales rather than loan security, the claimant is barred from asserting a higher value than the deed price, and the finding rejecting the oral price variation is upheld.

**Recurring facts:** A written sale deed or sale agreement states the price and the terms of the sale.; One party offers a different account of the price or of the transaction's nature (a loan or security arrangement, an oral higher price, or a higher stamp valuation).; The contrary account is oral or extrinsic and is not backed by persuasive evidence.

**Provisions:** Section 92, Indian Evidence Act, 1872; Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan, (2005) 6 SCC 243 (cited for reading agreements as a whole)

**Exceptions/limits:** Section 92 of the Evidence Act bars contrary evidence only as between parties to the document (and their representatives); the members do not address its application to strangers.; A contrary account can succeed only if it is supported by persuasive evidence; in the loan-versus-sale member the Court rejected the contrary account because it rested on vague oral testimony and conjecture.; The members do not discuss the statutory provisos to Section 92 (such as fraud or mistake), so the rule should not be read as deciding how they apply.; In one member the bar was also tied to the claimant having undervalued the document for stamp-duty purposes, and in another to concurrent fact findings that the Court declined to disturb.

## 403.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a court invoke its inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to grant relief, such as restoration, setting aside or recall of a decree or order, where the Code already provides an express procedure or an effective remedy for that situation?

**Rule:** IF `inherent_power_invoked_under_section_151 and code_provides_express_procedure_or_effective_remedy_for_the_situation and (requested_relief_falls_outside_that_remedy or requirements_of_that_remedy_not_met or party_could_have_used_that_remedy_instead)` THEN `inherent_power_cannot_be_used_to_grant_the_relief`

**Definition:** Inherent powers under Section 151 CPC cannot override or supplement express provisions of the Code. Where the Code supplies an express procedure or an effective remedy covering the situation, inherent powers cannot be used to create an additional remedy, to bypass the procedure when its requirements are unmet, or to substitute for an available remedy such as an appeal.

- `inherent_power_invoked_under_section_151`: The applicant asks the court to exercise its inherent powers under Section 151 CPC to grant relief (restoration, setting aside, or recall).
- `code_provides_express_procedure_or_effective_remedy_for_the_situation`: The Code of Civil Procedure expressly provides a procedure, or an effective alternative remedy such as an appeal, that covers the situation (for example Order IX rules 7 and 13, Order 37 rule 4, or an appeal under Section 96).
- `requested_relief_falls_outside_that_remedy`: The relief sought goes beyond or is different from what the provided procedure allows, so it would create an additional remedy.
- `requirements_of_that_remedy_not_met`: The conditions or circumstances the express procedure requires for the relief are not satisfied on the facts.
- `party_could_have_used_that_remedy_instead`: The applicant had an available alternative remedy, such as an appeal with leave, but chose to seek relief under inherent powers.
- `inherent_power_cannot_be_used_to_grant_the_relief`: The court may not use Section 151 inherent powers to grant the requested relief, and an order granting it is improper.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** In all 3 members, the Court refused to allow inherent powers to be used because the Code's express provisions or an available remedy governed the situation.

**Recurring facts:** An applicant sought relief from a decree or from the consequences of non-appearance by invoking Section 151 CPC.; The Code contained a specific provision or remedy covering the situation (Order IX rules 7 and 13, Order 37 rule 4, or an appeal under Section 96).; The applicant either did not satisfy that remedy's requirements, sought relief beyond it, or did not use it.

**Provisions:** Section 151 CPC; Order IX rules 7 and 13 CPC; Order 37 rule 4 CPC; Section 96 CPC

**Exceptions/limits:** Inherent powers remain available only in exceptional circumstances for which the Code lays down no procedure.; A court may still recall an order obtained by fraud on the court. The restriction applies where another effective remedy is available (1608703_5 and 463058_1 do not address this; 93015634_2 states it).

## 339.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Under Article 133 of the Constitution, when is a High Court certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court justified or competent where the civil case meets the property-value requirement, whether directly or through a claim or question indirectly respecting property of the required value?

**Rule:** IF `civil_appeal_certificate_proceeding and (direct_or_indirect_property_value_requirement_met) and (substantial_question_of_law_involved or valuation_route_requirements_satisfied)` THEN `certificate_for_appeal_is_justified`

**Definition:** A High Court certificate for appeal under Article 133 is justified where the case meets the property-value requirement. That requirement may be met by the subject matter itself, or by property of the required value that the judgment indirectly concerns. In addition, either a substantial question of law is involved or the valuation requirements of the applicable clause are satisfied. Real value may be considered independently of the plaint valuation where the plaint need not state market value.

- `civil_appeal_certificate_proceeding`: The matter is a civil proceeding in which a High Court has granted, or is asked to grant, a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133.
- `direct_or_indirect_property_value_requirement_met`: The subject matter in dispute, or the property directly or indirectly affected by the judgment or claim, has a real value above the threshold required by Article 133, even if the plaint valuation was lower because it was not required to use market value.
- `substantial_question_of_law_involved`: The case involves a substantial question of law, for example one certified by the High Court.
- `valuation_route_requirements_satisfied`: The valuation requirements of the applicable Article 133 clause are met: either the subject matter in the court of first instance and on appeal exceeds the threshold, or the judgment involves a claim or question respecting property of the required value that is other than the subject matter of the dispute.
- `certificate_for_appeal_is_justified`: The certificate for appeal is properly granted and the appeal is competent or maintainable.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members uphold the certificate or the maintainability of the appeal because the value requirement was met.

**Recurring facts:** High Court granted a certificate under Article 133; Property value, real or indirectly affected, exceeded the statutory threshold; The dispute's nominal subject matter or plaint valuation differed from the real value of the property concerned

**Provisions:** Constitution of India, Article 133; Article 133(1)(a) and (b)

**Exceptions/limits:** Under Article 133(1)(a), the value is that of the subject matter at first instance that is still in dispute on appeal.; The route under Article 133(1)(b), a claim or question respecting property, requires property additional to or other than the subject matter of the dispute.; Where the decree affirms the lower court's decision, a substantial question of law is needed (as indicated by 60827_1).; A case that does not involve a claim respecting property of the required value falls outside the rule.

## 360.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** How is limitation applied to post-sale applications in execution of a decree (an auction purchaser's application for delivery of possession, or an application to set aside the sale), and can later proceedings or general extension provisions postpone or enlarge the prescribed period?

**Rule:** IF `execution_sale_post_sale_application and filed_beyond_period_prescribed_by_specific_limitation_article and not (period_fixed_by_court_under_section_148 or later_proceeding_was_maintainable_and_affected_sale_becoming_absolute)` THEN `application_is_time_barred_and_period_not_extended_or_restarted`

**Definition:** Post-sale applications in execution are governed by their own specific limitation articles (Article 134 for purchaser's possession, Article 127 for setting aside a sale). Section 5 of the Limitation Act is excluded for Order XXI applications, Section 148 helps only where the court fixed the time, and an unmaintainable later challenge does not postpone the period, so late applications are barred.

- `execution_sale_post_sale_application`: The application is made in execution proceedings after an execution sale, either by the auction purchaser for delivery of possession or by a party to set aside the sale.
- `filed_beyond_period_prescribed_by_specific_limitation_article`: The application was filed after the period prescribed by the specific Limitation Act article for that kind of application (for example Article 134 for purchaser's delivery of possession, running from when the sale becomes absolute, or Article 127 for setting aside a sale, running from the date of sale).
- `period_fixed_by_court_under_section_148`: The court itself fixed the time for making the application or deposit, so that Section 148 of the Code can enlarge the time.
- `later_proceeding_was_maintainable_and_affected_sale_becoming_absolute`: A later application or appeal was legally maintainable and was a proceeding that could affect when the sale became absolute, so it could postpone the start of the limitation period.
- `application_is_time_barred_and_period_not_extended_or_restarted`: The application is barred by limitation; neither a general extension provision, an unmaintainable later challenge nor the execution forum provisions extend or restart the period, and the executing court cannot entertain it.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold the application time-barred or the period not extended: Article 134 governs the purchaser's possession application, a later unmaintainable challenge does not restart it, and the executing court cannot entertain a late application to set aside the sale.

**Recurring facts:** An execution sale of immovable property had taken place.; The post-sale application was filed after the prescribed period.; Attempts were made to avoid the bar by relying on the decree-execution article, a later application, or court-allowed time.

**Provisions:** Limitation Act, 1963, Articles 127, 134 and 136; Limitation Act, 1963, Section 5; Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXI Rules 89, 90, 91, 92 and 95; Code of Civil Procedure, Sections 47 and 148

**Exceptions/limits:** Time may be enlarged under Section 148 of the Code only where the court fixed the period for the application.; A maintainable proceeding, such as an appeal against an order refusing to set aside the sale, may affect when the sale becomes absolute and so when Article 134 starts to run.; The members concern different applications (purchaser's possession versus setting aside of sale), so the specific article and its starting point must be matched to the application.

**Split suggestion:** If a narrower grouping is wanted, separate the auction purchaser's possession limitation issues (1632704_1, 1632704_2, under Article 134) from the judgment-debtor's application to set aside a sale (1801026_1, under Article 127 and Section 148).

## 433.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** When a guardian disposes of or compromises a minor's rights without prior court permission, is the transaction invalid, or can it be validated by later court sanction, by the court's recorded finding of benefit, or by the minor's election after attaining majority?

**Rule:** IF `minor_interest_affected_by_guardian_transaction and (court_sanction_with_benefit_finding_recorded or (minor_reached_majority_during_proceedings and minor_elected_to_abide))` THEN `transaction_not_invalid_for_lack_of_prior_permission`

**Definition:** A guardian's disposition or compromise affecting a minor made without prior court permission is voidable at the minor's option, not void. It is validated where the court later sanctions it and records that it benefits the minor (no prescribed form is needed), or where the minor, on attaining majority during the proceedings, elects to abide by it.

- `minor_interest_affected_by_guardian_transaction`: A guardian or next friend has entered into an agreement, disposition or compromise that affects a minor's property or rights.
- `court_sanction_with_benefit_finding_recorded`: The court, in the proceedings, granted permission or sanction for the compromise and recorded that it was for the minor's benefit, in any form of words.
- `minor_reached_majority_during_proceedings`: The minor attained majority while the proceedings were pending.
- `minor_elected_to_abide`: On attaining majority, the former minor adopted or affirmed the agreement and expressed willingness to perform it.
- `transaction_not_invalid_for_lack_of_prior_permission`: The absence of prior court permission does not make the transaction void or unenforceable; it is voidable only, and it binds the minor once validated by later sanction or election.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members uphold the transaction or sanction against the challenge: absence of prior permission does not make the transaction void, and the defect is cured by later sanction or the minor's election.

**Recurring facts:** A guardian acted for a minor in an agreement or compromise without prior court permission or sanction.; A later event cured the defect: court sanction with a benefit finding, or the minor's affirmation on reaching majority.; The transaction was challenged as invalid for want of permission or for the form of sanction.

**Provisions:** Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, sections 8(2) and 8(3); Code of Civil Procedure, Order 32 rule 7 (including sub-rule (2))

**Exceptions/limits:** Where the minor repudiates the transaction, an unsanctioned agreement remains voidable at the minor's option.; The minor-election route was applied where the counterparty had not called on the guardian in writing to obtain permission; the members do not decide the position if such a request had been made.; The compromise route requires that the court actually sanction the compromise and be satisfied that it benefits the minor; the court's satisfaction must be recorded, though no particular form is required.; The members rest on section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (property dispositions) and Order 32 rule 7 of the CPC (compromises); they should not be applied across the two regimes without checking the specific provision.

## 4.7 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a party succeed on a factual claim or contention that was not pleaded or raised before the lower authorities or court, and that the record does not substantiate?

**Rule:** IF `factual_claim_asserted_on_appeal_or_later_stage and (claim_not_pleaded_or_not_raised_below) and record_does_not_establish_factual_basis` THEN `claim_not_established_and_rejected_or_not_adjudicated`

**Definition:** A party cannot obtain relief on a factual contention that was not properly pleaded or raised before the lower forum and that the record does not support. The court will reject the claim as unestablished or decline to make a finding on it.

- `factual_claim_asserted_on_appeal_or_later_stage`: A party relies on a factual claim or contention, in a land-related dispute, at a later stage (appeal, further proceedings or argument) to obtain relief.
- `claim_not_pleaded_or_not_raised_below`: The claim was not pleaded with the necessary specifics (such as the comparator, allotment or possession) or was not shown to have been raised before the lower authority, trial court or deciding judge.
- `record_does_not_establish_factual_basis`: The record, including pleadings and affidavits, does not contain the facts needed to decide the claim in the party's favour, and the court's record of what was argued is taken as correct.
- `claim_not_established_and_rejected_or_not_adjudicated`: The court rejects the claim as unproven, or declines to make a finding on it.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members decline relief on the unpleaded or unsubstantiated factual claim. Two reject the claim as not established, and one declines to make a finding and expresses no opinion.

**Recurring facts:** A land-related claim is made that was not pleaded with particulars or not raised before the lower authority or judge.; The record or pleadings lack the facts needed to decide the claim.; The opposing party denied the factual assertion, or the pleadings were silent on it.

**Provisions:** No specific statutory provision is relied on by the members; the land-reform law is only the setting of one issue.

**Exceptions/limits:** The outcome differs where the claim was pleaded with sufficient particulars or was shown to have been raised below, for example through a review application against the judge's record.; Where the record itself establishes the facts, the court may decide the claim.; The members differ in outcome: one declines to express any opinion on the claim, while the others reject it on the merits as unproven.; None of the members states a statutory basis for the rule.

**Split suggestion:** The members share the principle that unpleaded or unraised factual claims unsupported by the record fail. They could be split into (a) claims not raised below, where the court declines a finding (1646657_4 and 173339_1), and (b) unpleaded claims that cannot be proved beyond the pleadings (745891_2).

## 342.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Is the Government's discretion under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to withdraw from an acquisition (particularly one for a company or society beneficiary) open to judicial review, and is a withdrawal invalid if exercised arbitrarily, mala fide, on a mistaken basis, or on reasons not stated in the decision?

**Rule:** IF `challenge_to_withdrawal_from_acquisition and (withdrawal_arbitrary_or_mala_fide or withdrawal_based_on_mistaken_or_unsupported_reason or withdrawal_justified_only_by_later_reasons)` THEN `withdrawal_reviewable_and_liable_to_be_set_aside`

**Definition:** The State's power to withdraw from an acquisition under Section 48 is not absolute and is judicially reviewable. A withdrawal that is arbitrary, mala fide, based on a mistaken understanding, or supported only by reasons different from those on which it was made can be set aside.

- `challenge_to_withdrawal_from_acquisition`: A party, typically the beneficiary company or society, challenges the State's decision to withdraw from or release land from an acquisition.
- `withdrawal_arbitrary_or_mala_fide`: The withdrawal was made arbitrarily or in bad faith, without proper application of mind or proper verification.
- `withdrawal_based_on_mistaken_or_unsupported_reason`: The reason for withdrawal rests on a misconception of law or fact, or on a ground already considered and rejected, or one that cannot be sustained.
- `withdrawal_justified_only_by_later_reasons`: The withdrawal order or notification gives no reason or a different reason, and the State seeks to support it with new grounds raised later, for example in an affidavit.
- `withdrawal_reviewable_and_liable_to_be_set_aside`: The withdrawal decision is subject to judicial review and may be held arbitrary and invalid and set aside, with the State free to reconsider according to law.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 hold the withdrawal power is reviewable and not absolute; 2 set the withdrawal aside as arbitrary and 1 resolves the challenge on a lack of opportunity to the company.

**Recurring facts:** Housing scheme or society acquisition under the company-acquisition provisions, with the beneficiary challenging the withdrawal.; State withdrew or released land at the instance of landowners or on a stated or later-asserted reason.; Withdrawal likely to prejudice the beneficiary's interests.; The reason offered for withdrawal was erroneous, unexplained or unverified.

**Provisions:** Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (and Section 48(2) compensation); Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (declaration conclusive as to public purpose); Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (acquisition for companies)

**Exceptions/limits:** The State's discretion is wide, and review is limited to arbitrariness or mala fides; withdrawal is not unreviewable but is not invalid merely because it is a withdrawal.; In 1788830_9 the Court recognised prejudice to the company beneficiary but resolved the challenge on lack of opportunity to respond, so the outcome there is more procedural.; Where the withdrawal is challenged by a landowner, the distinction in Amarnath Ashram and Godrej & Boyce is relevant; the cases do not establish unreviewable discretion.; The Court left open whether withdrawal from a company acquisition requires the company's consent.; Possession having been taken is relevant to the Section 48 power, which operates before possession.; A public purpose finding in a Section 6 declaration cannot be reopened by the State or by owners who withdrew their challenge.

## 343.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Where a landlord sends a properly addressed, prepaid registered notice demanding rent arrears, does the statutory presumption of postal service make the notice effective (including where the tenant refuses it or it is returned undelivered), so that the statutory notice requirement is met and the tenant is imputed with knowledge of its contents?

**Rule:** IF `rent_eviction_proceeding and notice_properly_addressed_prepaid_and_sent_by_registered_post and postal_tender_attempted_at_correct_address and not postal_service_presumption_rebutted` THEN `notice_treated_as_effectively_served_and_statutory_notice_requirement_satisfied`

**Definition:** A correctly addressed, prepaid registered notice sent by the landlord raises a rebuttable presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act and section 114 illustration (f) of the Evidence Act. If the postal worker tendered it and it was refused, service is effective and the tenant is imputed with knowledge of its contents, without any need to open or read it. If it was returned undelivered, sending it satisfies a statutory requirement that the landlord send notice by post, and actual receipt is not required.

- `rent_eviction_proceeding`: The dispute is an eviction proceeding against a tenant under a rent control statute based on non-payment of rent or arrears.
- `notice_properly_addressed_prepaid_and_sent_by_registered_post`: The landlord sent a notice demanding rent arrears by registered post, correctly addressed to the tenant and with postage prepaid.
- `postal_tender_attempted_at_correct_address`: The postal worker tendered or attempted to tender the letter to the tenant at the correct address, whether the tenant refused it or could not be found.
- `postal_service_presumption_rebutted`: The tenant has successfully rebutted the presumption of postal service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act or section 114 illustration (f) of the Evidence Act.
- `notice_treated_as_effectively_served_and_statutory_notice_requirement_satisfied`: The notice counts as effectively served and the statutory notice requirement is met. Where the tenant refused it, the tenant is imputed with knowledge of its contents, so that non-compliance with the demand can amount to wilful default.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold the notice effectively served or the notice requirement satisfied, in favour of the landlord. In 2 of them, refusal imputes knowledge of the contents, supporting wilful default.

**Recurring facts:** Landlord sent a registered notice demanding rent arrears to the tenant at the correct address; Postman tendered the notice, and the tenant either refused it or could not be found; Tenant did not comply with the demand; The dispute arose in a rent control eviction proceeding

**Provisions:** Section 27, General Clauses Act, 1897; Section 114, Illustration (f), Indian Evidence Act; Section 14(a) of the applicable rent control Act (wilful default); Sections 11(1)(i) proviso and 12(3) proviso, Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966

**Exceptions/limits:** The presumption of service is rebuttable. If the tenant rebuts it, the outcome may differ.; Wilful default requires that the tenant failed to pay within the time allowed after the notice (for example one month). Effective service alone does not establish default (1821913_1).; The returned-notice holding (981029_1) rests on statutory wording requiring that notice be sent by post. It may not extend to statutes that require actual delivery or receipt.; Tender at the correct address is essential. Refusal must be proved, here by the postman's testimony accepted by the courts.

## 346.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can a higher reviewing authority (a writ court or a statutory revisional authority) set aside concurrent or subordinate factual findings of consolidation or administrative authorities where those findings are supported by evidence and official records, and the reviewing authority has reversed them without a legally sustainable basis such as ignoring material evidence?

**Rule:** IF `reviewing_authority_reverses_factual_findings_of_subordinate_authorities and findings_supported_by_evidence_or_official_records and (findings_are_concurrent or reviewing_authority_ignored_material_evidence) and not reviewing_authority_has_legally_sustainable_ground_to_interfere` THEN `reversal_unjustified_and_subordinate_findings_stand_or_are_restored`

**Definition:** A writ court under Articles 226/227 or a statutory revisional authority may not reopen or reverse factual findings of consolidation or administrative authorities that are concurrent and supported by evidence and official records, nor reverse them by ignoring vital evidence. Where it does, the reversal is set aside and the subordinate findings stand or are restored.

- `reviewing_authority_reverses_factual_findings_of_subordinate_authorities`: A writ court or revisional authority has set aside, or is asked to set aside, factual findings made by subordinate consolidation or administrative authorities.
- `findings_supported_by_evidence_or_official_records`: The subordinate findings rest on clear or material evidence and/or official records, such as records of right, revenue receipts or genuine undisputed documents.
- `findings_are_concurrent`: Two or more subordinate authorities have reached the same factual finding.
- `reviewing_authority_ignored_material_evidence`: The reviewing authority overlooked or disregarded vital evidence, or wrongly treated a genuine undisputed record as fabricated, in reversing the findings.
- `reviewing_authority_has_legally_sustainable_ground_to_interfere`: The reviewing authority can point to a recognised legal ground for interference, such as a finding unsupported by any evidence or a manifest error of law, that does not depend on re-weighing the facts.
- `reversal_unjustified_and_subordinate_findings_stand_or_are_restored`: The reviewing authority's interference is not justified, and the subordinate findings are left undisturbed or restored to the extent the evidence supports them.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold the reversal or reopening of factual findings unjustified: 2 set aside the High Court's or revisional authority's reversal and restore the subordinate findings, and 1 upholds the High Court's refusal to reopen concurrent findings in a writ petition.

**Recurring facts:** Consolidation or administrative authorities made factual findings on possession, title or entitlement.; The findings were supported by evidence and official records (records of right, revenue receipts, genuine documents, genealogy).; A higher authority (High Court in writ jurisdiction, or Deputy Director in revision) reversed or sought to reopen those findings.

**Provisions:** Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India; Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953

**Exceptions/limits:** A revisional authority may interfere where material admissible evidence was overlooked or the finding is unsupported by evidence, but it may not re-weigh the facts de novo.; The writ court's restraint is tied to concurrence of findings and their support in evidence and records; it does not bar interference where there is no evidentiary support or there is a legal error.; The restoration is limited to the extent the findings are supported by the evidence (e.g. the half share in one member).

## 349.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Under the Arbitration Act, 1940, can an arbitrator or a court act outside the limits of the arbitrator's authority, as fixed by the agreement, the court's reference and the rule that the arbitrator is functus officio once the award is made?

**Rule:** IF `arbitration_under_1940_act and (arbitrator_authority_limited_by_agreement_or_reference) and (arbitrator_award_or_direction_goes_beyond_reference_or_conferred_powers or court_directs_arbitrator_to_act_again_after_award_made) and no_further_reference_or_conferral_of_power` THEN `act_is_beyond_jurisdiction_and_not_sustainable`

**Definition:** Under the Arbitration Act, 1940, an arbitrator is a tribunal of limited jurisdiction, confined to the agreement and the court's reference. Relief or interim directions beyond that scope, absent a further reference or conferred power, are without jurisdiction. Neither consent nor a court's inherent power can authorise an arbitrator to act afresh after the award has been made.

- `arbitration_under_1940_act`: The arbitration or related court proceeding is governed by the Arbitration Act, 1940.
- `arbitrator_authority_limited_by_agreement_or_reference`: The arbitrator's authority is confined to the arbitration agreement and, where the court referred the matter, to the reference made by the court.
- `arbitrator_award_or_direction_goes_beyond_reference_or_conferred_powers`: The arbitrator has awarded relief, entertained a fresh claim or issued an interim direction beyond the claim referred or the powers conferred by the agreement.
- `court_directs_arbitrator_to_act_again_after_award_made`: After the arbitrator made the award, the court directed the arbitrator to prepare or make a fresh award or resubmit it, relying on inherent or procedural power.
- `no_further_reference_or_conferral_of_power`: There is no further court order of reference and no agreement conferring the power exercised, and party consent cannot supply it.
- `act_is_beyond_jurisdiction_and_not_sustainable`: The arbitrator's award or direction, or the court's direction, is outside jurisdiction. The excess is not sustained, the award is confined to the referred claim, and the direction cannot support later proceedings.

**Coherence:** medium · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members hold the act beyond jurisdiction. In one the award is capped at the referred claim, in one the court's direction for a fresh award is invalid, and in one the interim direction is a nullity.

**Recurring facts:** Arbitration was conducted under the Arbitration Act, 1940.; The arbitrator or the court took a step beyond the scope of the reference or the arbitrator's powers.; The excess consisted of an enlarged claim, an interim direction or a fresh award after the award was made.

**Provisions:** Arbitration Act, 1940, sections 20(1) and 20(4); Arbitration Act, 1940, section 41 and the Second Schedule; Code of Civil Procedure, section 151; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, section 17 (contrast)

**Exceptions/limits:** The arbitrator may act beyond the original reference if the court makes a further order of reference or the agreement confers the power.; The rule is tied to the 1940 Act. The 1996 Act expressly confers limited interim-measure powers on arbitrators under section 17.; The functus officio point concerns a court's inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It does not address statutory powers to remit or modify an award.

**Split suggestion:** Optionally split into (a) arbitrator exceeding the reference or agreed powers (171331_1, 231673_1) and (b) court direction to a functus officio arbitrator (1791303_2).

## 350.0 (3 issues)

**Question:** Can graves be relocated despite objections based on religious freedom or the sanctity of graves, where relocation is a necessary and feasible measure to prevent recurring sectarian violence and maintain public order?

**Rule:** IF `religious_freedom_or_desecration_challenge_to_grave_relocation and recurring_sectarian_violence_or_disorder_risk and relocation_is_necessary_and_feasible_to_maintain_public_order and no_adequate_less_drastic_alternative_available` THEN `grave_relocation_upheld_as_consistent_with_religious_freedom`

**Definition:** Religious freedoms under Articles 25 and 26 are subject to public order, and the sanctity of graves is not absolute. Graves may be relocated where recurring sectarian violence makes relocation a necessary and feasible measure, no adequate lesser alternative exists, and no scriptural prohibition on necessary relocation is shown.

- `religious_freedom_or_desecration_challenge_to_grave_relocation`: The relocation of graves is challenged as violating constitutional religious freedoms (Articles 25 and 26) or as being religiously prohibited or a desecration.
- `recurring_sectarian_violence_or_disorder_risk`: Religious ceremonies of rival communities at the site have repeatedly involved violence or a real apprehension of violence and disorder.
- `relocation_is_necessary_and_feasible_to_maintain_public_order`: Moving the graves is practicable and is needed to separate the communities' worship areas and reduce the risk of further violence, so a stated necessity exists.
- `no_adequate_less_drastic_alternative_available`: Alternatives to relocation have been tried or suggested and failed or been rejected, leaving no adequate less drastic solution.
- `grave_relocation_upheld_as_consistent_with_religious_freedom`: The court holds that the relocation direction does not violate religious freedoms, is not shown to be religiously prohibited or a desecration, and is justified by public order.

**Coherence:** high · covered 3/3 shown · outliers 0

**Typical outcome:** All 3 members reject the challenge and permit relocation on public-order grounds.

**Recurring facts:** Rival religious communities or sects conducting ceremonies at the same site; Repeated violence or apprehension of violence during ceremonies; Graves placed contrary to a court order or injunction; Relocation of graves proposed or directed to separate worship areas; Objection that relocation violates religion or desecrates graves

**Provisions:** Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution; Section 176(3) Code of Criminal Procedure (exhumation shows interred bodies are not immune); Section 144 Code of Criminal Procedure (history of restrictions)

**Exceptions/limits:** Relocation must be necessary and feasible; the religious edict relied on in one member prohibits only unnecessary relocation, so unnecessary relocation is not covered.; The petitioner's religious-prohibition argument fails only where no scriptural prohibition on necessary relocation is identified; a shown prohibition could change the analysis.; Rights remain protected where less drastic measures could adequately maintain public order.; Members stress that graves had been placed in defiance of a court order or injunction; the rule's application where graves were lawfully placed is not addressed.

## 6.7 (3 issues)

**Question:** When may a High Court set aside an acquittal (on appeal or in revision) and order a retrial or continuation of the trial, and what kind of defect in the acquittal or the trial is needed to justify it?

**Rule:** IF `high_court_asked_to_interfere_with_acquittal and acquittal_suffers_from_legal_defect_beyond_mere_reappraisal_of_evidence and justice_requires_intervention` THEN `high_court_may_set_aside_acquittal_and_order_retrial_or_further_proceedings`

**Definition:** A High Court may set aside an acquittal and order a retrial or continuation of the trial only where the acquittal is marred by a real legal or jurisdictional defect (such as an uncharged serious offence or invalid compounding) and justice requires it. It may not do so merely by reweighing the evidence and substituting its own view.

- `high_court_asked_to_interfere_with_acquittal`: A High Court is exercising appellate power (against acquittal) or revisional power over an acquittal passed by a subordinate criminal court.
- `acquittal_suffers_from_legal_defect_beyond_mere_reappraisal_of_evidence`: The acquittal is vitiated by a substantive legal or jurisdictional defect, such as an omitted serious offence that would take the case beyond the trial court's jurisdiction, or compounding of an offence that the law does not allow to be compounded, amounting to manifest illegality or gross miscarriage of justice, and not merely a different view of the evidence.
- `justice_requires_intervention`: The justice of the case clearly demands that the acquittal be set aside, the power being used sparingly and with great care.
